+
+## Strongest mathematical operation
+
+Let T be a compactly supported finite-order Hermitian d-by-d matrix-valued
+distribution on R^m, with total mass T(1)=I. A distribution here permits signed
+densities and derivatives of delta masses. Define its real Laplace transform
+
+    L_T(g)=<T(y), exp(g·y)>,       g in R^m.
+
+The internally proved criterion is:
+
+    L_T(g) is positive definite for every real g
+    iff some scalar probability noise with every exponential moment
+        makes T*noise a positive matrix distribution.
+
+Whenever this is possible, the noise can be a single smooth radial strictly
+log-concave density p. The result T*p is then positive definite at every
+point, normalized to I, and has every exponential moment, as do its derivatives.
+The noise depends on T. This is pointwise matrix positivity of L_T(g), not
+Bochner positive-definiteness of a function on a group. Semidefinite transforms
+with zeros do not suffice for normalized mass I. The proof also treats singular
+matrix masses using a constant-kernel condition, and general Banach cones with
+an interior normalization under its stated norm-distribution hypotheses.
+
+The construction retains the positive exponential tangent L_T(grad V(x)) and
+expands only the local curvature remainder of p=exp(-V)/Z. Unlike the supplied
+quantum-tuple result, it assumes no exponential lower bound on the Laplace
+positivity margin. An explicit sequence of smooth slope transitions makes
+curvature decay fast enough relative to the worst margin on each gradient
+ball, while the slope still diverges. Thus p has every exponential moment.
+The necessity proof uses compact cutoffs and works even for probability noise
+without a density; positive output forces strict transform positivity.
+
+The difference in hypotheses is real. A compact smooth signed scalar kernel
+is constructed whose real Laplace transform is everywhere positive but has
+valleys below exp[-exp(r_n²)] along an explicit sequence. Any positive
+regularization forces noise cumulant growth at least exp(r_n²)-O(r_n).
+Consequently no density bounded in both tails by C exp[-c|x|log|x|], for any
+c>0, can regularize it. The adaptive all-exponential-moment construction still
+does. This is an analytic example, not a numerically resolved tiny valley.
+
+Evidence: [full proof](workers/mathematical_invention/PROOF.md),
+[producer report](workers/mathematical_invention/REPORT.md), and
+[independent construction](workers/laplace_consequences/REPORT.txt).
+The latter uses a different sum-of-square-root potentials and an independent

+## Closest mathematics and the remaining consequence
+
+Positive convolution multipliers are established mathematics. The accessible
+Katkova–Vishnyakova 2001 theorem already obtains a nonnegative scalar
+convolution from strict bilateral Laplace positivity for a compact-interval
+input positive at both endpoints, without a quantitative global transform
+margin. Its multiplier is one-sided and atomic. The proposed smooth compact
+examples have zero support-boundary values, and the current target additionally
+specifies radial strict log-concavity, arbitrary dimension, matrix/cone values
+and strict all-space output. These differences do not establish priority.
+
+Diamond–Essén, *Functions with non-negative convolutions* (1978), is a decisive
+older predecessor. Its publication was verified, but its exact theorem text
+could not be retrieved through the accessible publisher routes. **Historical
+novelty is UNKNOWN.** Poincaré–Pólya–Handelman coefficient/multiplier results
+and matrix polynomial positivity certificates are additional close precedents.
+[Exact comparison and access limits](workers/laplace_literature/PRIMARY_COMPARISON.md).
+
+The mathematical consequence is an exact existence criterion and new-to-this-
+investigation constructions for positive representations of signed distributions
+and constant-coefficient differential operations. It does not decide positivity
+of an arbitrary symbol, give an efficient kernel compiler, optimize variance,
+stabilize deconvolution, or establish a computational speedup. Thresholds may
+be enormous and require supplied lower margins on entire real gradient balls.
+The next proof with operational consequence would turn specified computable
+margin/seminorm bounds into finite-precision, finite-cost constructions with
+useful noise and sampling bounds. Exact comparison with Diamond–Essén is
+required before making a priority claim; specialist proof review is open.

+constructor obtained a direct compiler: sample r with density 4pi r²u(r),
+measure a uniformly random spin direction once, and classically flip the
+resulting direction with mean v/u. This avoids estimating a Fourier transform
+from many copies. The gamma kernel in the pasted input was reconstructed;
+its existence was supplied, not newly invented here.

+existing covariant spin POVM. That incumbent statistically dominates its
+output for every state-inference decision. Hence the compiler supplies the
+requested exact projection-law format without an information-acquisition
+advantage under the same random-axis interface. Its raw coordinate second
+moment is about 8.639917, versus 3 for the ordinary covariant 3n estimator or

+continuous rotations are not certified finite-precision hardware.

+ASTRA FOUNDATIONAL MATHEMATICS GENESIS — Discover a New Source of Mathematical Power

+

+Result: a universal positive representation with superexponential noise
+I developed a proof of a universal positive regularization theorem for bounded noncommuting observables, together with a matching obstruction that identifies the sharp leading radial tail scale.
+The central finding is that dependence between noise coordinates can supply a mathematical capability that their individual distributions and covariance do not reveal. The construction works with noise having every exponential moment—outside the scope of Astra’s previous successful independent-noise construction.
+The proof uses a different operation: retain an exact positive exponential tilt, and control only the nonlinear remainder of the logarithm of the noise density.
+The argument and reproducible checks are preserved here:
+PROOF.md · CHECKPOINT.md · astra_tilt_regularization_2026-10-15.zip
+Status: this is an internally derived, proof-backed research candidate. It has not been independently reviewed or formally verified, and historical priority remains unresolved. It does not yet establish a major computational or technological capability.
+1. The mathematical obstruction selected
+After screening identity testing, quantum recovery, and sampling-related directions, I concentrated on a precise representation problem:
+Can one positive measurement produce a classical vector whose every linear projection reproduces the corresponding quantum observable, with a prescribed state-independent additive noise?
+
+Let \(A_1,\ldots,A_m\) be bounded self-adjoint operators and write
+\[
+A(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{m}t_jA_j.
+\]
+For a classical noise density \(p\), seek a positive operator-valued probability density \(M_A\) satisfying
+\[
+\boxed{
+\int_{\mathbb R^m}e^{it\cdot x}M_A(x)\,dx
+=
+\widehat p(t)e^{iA(t)}.
+}
+\tag{1}
+\]
+Here
+\[
+M_A(x)\succeq0,\qquad \int M_A(x)\,dx=I.
+\]
+For a quantum state \(\rho\), the classical output has density
+\[
+P_\rho(x)=\operatorname{tr}\!\bigl(\rho M_A(x)\bigr).
+\]
+Equation (1) means that, for every real vector \(u\), the law of \(u\cdot X\) is exactly the spectral law of \(A(u)\), convolved with the law of \(u\cdot Z\), where \(Z\sim p\).
+This is stronger than jointly measuring noisy versions of the individual coordinates. The all-linear-marginal Wigner framework is established mathematics; I am not claiming that representation itself as new. Published particle-approximation work also constructs signed measures approaching it. DOI
+The opening in Astra’s previous result
+The earlier Astra note supplied two contrasting candidates: Gaussian noise permits this exact representation only for commuting bounded tuples, while sufficiently broad independent hyperbolic-secant noise permits it for arbitrary bounded tuples.    Pasted markdown(20261011-124622)
+Its stronger obstruction explicitly required independent noise coordinates: if one coordinate has every exponential moment and a transverse coordinate has finite variance, noncommutativity is impossible under that independence assumption.    Pasted markdown(20261011-124622)
+The new investigation challenges that assumption rather than trying to improve the old derivative expansion.
+The proposed escape is dependent, radially symmetric noise whose tails decay faster than every exponential, but not as fast as a Gaussian.
+2. Main theorem: one noise law for every bounded tuple
+Suppose a positive bound \(R\) is available such that
+\[
+\sup_{|u|=1}\|A(u)\|\le R.
+\]
+Choose
+\[
+0<c<\frac1{2R}.
+\]
+Define
+\[
+f(z)=\sqrt{1+|z|^2}\log\sqrt{1+|z|^2},
+\]
+and, for a scale \(L>0\),
+\[
+V_L(x)=cL f(x/L),\qquad
+p_L(x)=\frac{e^{-V_L(x)}}{\displaystyle\int e^{-V_L(y)}\,dy}.
+\]
+Universal regularization theorem
+For sufficiently large finite \(L\), depending only on \(m,R,c\), the inverse Fourier transform
+\[
+\boxed{
+M_{A,L}
+=
+\mathcal F^{-1}\!\left[
+\widehat p_L(t)e^{iA(t)}
+\right]
+}
+\tag{2}
+\]
+is a positive, normalized operator density for every tuple satisfying the norm bound.
+Moreover, writing \(g_L(x)=\nabla V_L(x)\),
+\[
+\boxed{
+\frac12\,p_L(x)e^{A(g_L(x))}
+\preceq M_{A,L}(x)
+\preceq
+\frac32\,p_L(x)e^{A(g_L(x))}.
+}
+\tag{3}
+\]
+The same scalar noise works uniformly over the operator tuple and independently of Hilbert-space dimension. The argument applies to bounded operators on infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces as well as finite matrices.
+The density is smooth, radial, and strictly log-concave. Its tails satisfy
+\[
+-\log p_L(x)
+=
+c|x|\log|x|+O(|x|),
+\]
+so
+\[
+\boxed{
+\int e^{a|x|}p_L(x)\,dx<\infty
+\quad\text{for every finite }a\ge0.
+}
+\tag{4}
+\]
+Thus this is not a heavy-tailed construction with missing moments. It has all polynomial moments and all exponential moments.
+The constants \(1/2\) and \(3/2\) in (3) can be replaced by \(1-\varepsilon\) and \(1+\varepsilon\) by increasing \(L\). However, the proof does not provide an optimized practical scale or a polynomial-time measurement compiler.
+3. The mathematical operation behind the theorem
+The essential change is what gets expanded.
+Astra’s previous successful construction controlled derivatives of \(p\) relative to \(p\), uniformly throughout the tails. That works for its hyperbolic-secant density.    Pasted markdown(20261011-124622)
+Here, \(\nabla\log p_L(x)\) becomes unbounded. Comparing the entire operator density with \(p_L(x)I\) is therefore the wrong representation.
+Instead, the comparison is with
+\[
+p_L(x)e^{A(\nabla V_L(x))},
+\]
+which is positive exactly, without assuming commutativity.
+Step 1: retain the generalized Wigner distribution
+Let \(W_A\) denote the operator-valued distribution with
+\[
+\widehat W_A(t)=e^{iA(t)}.
+\]
+Its support lies in the ball \(\overline B_R\). The relevant exponential-type estimate follows from
+\[
+\|e^{iA(t)-A(s)}\|\le e^{R|s|},
+\]
+followed by the standard Paley–Wiener–Schwartz support theorem.
+Crucially, its real Laplace transform is
+\[
+\boxed{
+\langle W_A,e^{g\cdot y}\rangle=e^{A(g)}\succ0.
+}
+\tag{5}
+\]
+The distribution itself need not be positive. Nevertheless, every real exponential test gives a strictly positive operator.
+There is also a distribution estimate independent of operator dimension. For a fixed cutoff \(\chi\) supported in a slightly larger ball \(B_{R_1}\),
+\[
+\|\langle W_A,\chi h\rangle\|
+\le
+C\max_{|\alpha|\le N}
+\sup_{B_{R_1}}|\partial^\alpha h|,
+\tag{6}
+\]
+where a finite even \(N>m\) suffices.
+This is reconstructed directly from
+\[
+\|\langle W_A,h\rangle\|
+\le (2\pi)^{-m}\|\widehat h\|_1,
+\]
+and integration by parts using \((1-\Delta)^{N/2}\). It does not hide dimension-dependent matrix coefficients.
+Step 2: expand the logarithmic remainder, not the exponential tilt
+For each \(x\), set
+\[
+g=\nabla V_L(x),
+\]
+and define
+\[
+F_x(y)
+=
+V_L(x-y)-V_L(x)+g\cdot y.
+\]
+Then the following is exact:
+\[
+p_L(x-y)
+=
+p_L(x)e^{g\cdot y}e^{-F_x(y)}.
+\]
+Applying \(W_A\),
+\[
+\frac{M_{A,L}(x)}{p_L(x)}
+=
+e^{A(g)}+E_x,
+\]
+where
+\[
+E_x=
+\left\langle W_A,
+e^{g\cdot y}\bigl(e^{-F_x(y)}-1\bigr)
+\right\rangle,
+\]
+with a cutoff understood on the compact support.
+The whole noncommutative exponential is retained. Only the curvature remainder is treated perturbatively.
+Step 3: control that remainder everywhere
+Put
+\[
+s=\frac{|x|}{L},\qquad h(s)=1+\log(1+s).
+\]
+The chosen potential satisfies
+\[
+|g|\le c\,h(s),
+\]
+and, through the finitely many derivative orders needed in (6),
+\[
+\|F_x\|_{C^N(B_{R_1})}
+\le
+\frac{C}{L}\frac{h(s)}{1+s}.
+\]
+The logarithmic slope grows, but its local variation becomes small.
+The distribution estimate then yields
+\[
+\|E_x\|
+\le
+\frac{C}{L}
+e^{R_1|g|}(1+|g|)^N
+\frac{h(s)}{1+s}.
+\]
+An absolute error estimate is insufficient because the smallest eigenvalue of \(e^{A(g)}\) may be small. The error must be measured relative to the positive leading operator:
+\[
+\left\|
+e^{-A(g)/2}E_xe^{-A(g)/2}
+\right\|
+\le
+\frac{C'}{L}
+h(s)^{N+1}(1+s)^{-a},
+\tag{7}
+\]
+where
+\[
+a=1-c(R+R_1).
+\]
+Because \(c<1/(2R)\), one can choose \(R_1>R\) with \(a>0\). Therefore
+\[
+\sup_{s\ge0}
+h(s)^{N+1}(1+s)^{-a}<\infty.
+\]
+Taking \(L\) sufficiently large makes (7) at most \(1/2\), proving positivity at every point, including arbitrarily remote tails. Fourier evaluation at zero gives normalization.
+A broader principle
+The same proof applies to a compactly supported operator distribution \(T\) whose Laplace transform satisfies
+\[
+T(e^{g\cdot y})\succeq \eta e^{-b|g|}I,
+\]
+provided a finite distribution seminorm is controlled.
+If its support lies in \(B_a\), the construction works for
+\[
+c<\frac1{a+b}.
+\]
+This is the reusable candidate operation: turn quantitative Laplace positivity into genuine positivity after a carefully designed scalar convolution.
+It is not a claim that Laplace positivity alone, without the stated quantitative assumptions, solves every regularization problem.
+4. Matching obstruction: the \(r\log r\) scale is sharp
+An existence construction could still be an unnecessarily permissive workaround. To test that, I derived a converse using a noncommuting Pauli pair:
+\[
+A_1=R\sigma_z,\qquad A_2=R\sigma_x.
+\]
+Suppose a radial noise law admits the exact representation, and define its directional cumulant generating function
+\[
+K(s)=\log\mathbb E e^{sZ_1}.
+\]
+Exponentially tilt the proposed positive measurement in the first coordinate. Positivity of the resulting first- and second-moment block matrix forces
+\[
+\text{tilted transverse variance}
+\ge
+\frac{\sinh(2Rs)-2Rs}{2s^2}.
+\]
+For radial noise, the transverse variance under this tilt is exactly
+\[
+\frac{K'(s)}s.
+\]
+Consequently,
+\[
+\boxed{
+K'(s)\ge
+\frac{\sinh(2Rs)-2Rs}{2s}.
+}
+\tag{8}
+\]
+The right-hand side grows exponentially with rate \(2R\).
+Now suppose a radial density decays at least as fast as
+\[
+p(x)\le C e^{-c_0|x|\log|x|}
+\]
+for some
+\[
+c_0>\frac1{2R}.
+\]
+Choose \(c'\) strictly between \(1/(2R)\) and \(c_0\). The elementary optimization
+\[
+\sup_{r>0}\{sr-c'r\log r\}
+=
+c'e^{s/c'-1}
+\]
+bounds the cumulant growth by an exponential rate at most \(1/c'<2R\), contradicting (8).
+Exact universal supremum
+For \(m\ge2\), consider smooth radial noises satisfying
+\[
+-\log p(x)=c|x|\log|x|+O(|x|)
+\]
+that work for every bounded tuple with directional norm at most \(R\).
+The construction supplies every \(c<1/(2R)\). The Pauli obstruction excludes every \(c>1/(2R)\). Hence
+\[
+\boxed{
+\sup c_{\mathrm{universally\ admissible}}
+=
+\frac1{2R}.
+}
+\tag{9}
+\]
+This is a complete supremum statement, not a claim of universal attainment at equality.
+It also distinguishes two notions that can otherwise be confused:
+The noise can decay faster than every exponential, but cannot have arbitrarily fast radial tails. Radial Gaussian tails, for example, are too fast for this exact interface.
+This is an exact-positivity obstruction, not a lower bound on approximation error. The forbidden negativity can reside in regions carrying extremely small probability mass.
+5. A stronger separation: identical coordinate laws, opposite answers
+The construction gives a direct test of what information covariance and individual marginals omit.
+Let \(p_L\) be a successful radial noise and \(q_L\) its common one-coordinate marginal. Form the product density
+\[
+p_{\mathrm{prod}}(x)
+=
+\prod_{j=1}^{m}q_L(x_j).
+\]
+These two noise laws have:
+- exactly the same individual coordinate distributions;
+- the same mean and covariance matrix;
+- every exponential moment.
+Nevertheless, \(p_L\) supplies the exact representation for every tuple in the norm ball, whereas \(p_{\mathrm{prod}}\) cannot supply it for a noncommuting finite-dimensional tuple.
+The reason is precise. Under exponential tilting, dependence allows the transverse variance to grow. For the product law, that variance stays fixed while the noncommutative covariance defect diverges.
+Thus
+\[
+\boxed{
+\text{same coordinate laws and covariance}
+\;\not\Rightarrow\;
+\text{same exact all-linear representation capability}.
+}
+\tag{10}
+\]
+There is an important qualification: the noisy coordinate observables themselves still have a joint measurement, witnessed by the successful construction. What fails for the product noise is the stronger requirement that every linear projection have the prescribed noise-convolved law.
+The two noises do not have identical distributions in every projection; that would determine their joint law.
+6. An explicit endpoint example, rather than only an existence proof
+I also obtained a separate exact construction for the Pauli triple
+\[
+A=(\sigma_x,\sigma_y,\sigma_z).
+\]
+On \(\mathbb R^3\), take
+\[
+\boxed{
+p(x)=\frac{C}{\Gamma(2+|x|/2)}.
+}
+\tag{11}
+\]
+Its leading tail coefficient is \(1/2\), precisely the boundary for \(R=1\), and it has every exponential moment. This particular density is not smooth at the origin.
+The proof uses a radial wave formula. Write \(p(r)\) for its radial profile, \(f(r)=rp(r)\), and
+\[
+I(r)=\int_{|r-1|}^{r+1}f(s)\,ds.
+\]
+The operator kernel has the form
+\[
+M(x)=u(r)I+v(r)\widehat x\cdot\sigma.
+\]
+Its potentially problematic eigenvalue is
+\[
+u(r)-v(r)
+=
+\frac{f(r+1)}r-\frac{I(r)}{2r^2}.
+\]
+For \(r\ge1\), monotonicity of \(p\) and the gamma recurrence give
+\[
+I(r)\le2r\,p(r-1),
+\]
+and
+\[
+\frac{p(r-1)}{p(r+1)}
+=
+\frac{r+3}{2}
+\le r+1.
+\]
+Therefore \(I(r)\le2r f(r+1)\), proving that eigenvalue nonnegative. On \(0<r<1\), monotonicity of \(f\) on \([0,2]\) proves both eigenvalue inequalities.
+The Fourier identity and normalization follow from the spherical wave kernel.
+This example tests the mechanism without an unspecified large scale \(L\). It is not a substitute for the universal theorem, a variance optimum, or a proof of universal endpoint attainment.
+7. Tests performed—and a decisive failed candidate
+The numerical checks were executed, not merely proposed.

+

+This does not invalidate that learning hardware. It prevents us from importing the present theorem into it merely because its components are called resistors.
+2. What the operation actually acquires
+The recovered result assumes
+\[
+A=
+\begin{pmatrix}
+B&E\\
+E^T&C
+\end{pmatrix},
+\qquad C=C^T,
+\]
+with all nonreciprocity confined to known accessible coordinates selected by \(P\). At the same loaded operating point, it measures
+\[
+Y=A^{-1}P,\qquad z=A^{-1}c,\qquad H=P^TY,
+\]
+and solves
+\[
+H\alpha=P^Tz,\qquad
+H\beta=(H^T-H)\alpha.
+\]
+Then
+\[
+\boxed{\lambda=z+Y\beta=A^{-T}c.}
+\]
+This reconstructs the adjoint without separately identifying the reciprocal interior or every nonreciprocal component value. It still requires the physical sources, the necessary sensed rows, and the actual control derivatives.    RESEARCH_NOTE(20261015-020428)
+Advance 1: not every quantity needs reacquisition after an update
+The loaded port response determines
+\[
+\boxed{D=H^{-T}-H^{-1}=B^T-B.}
+\]
+Consequently,
+\[
+A^T=A+PDP^T.
+\]
+If control updates change only reciprocal elements and the nonreciprocal module’s response remains fixed, \(D\) remains fixed even though \(H\) changes.
+That is a useful correction to an overly broad claim that every relevant calibration must be repeated at every setting. The original digital formula needs the new \(H\), but the antisymmetric module response need not change with it.
+In the synthetic test, a reciprocal update changed \(H\) by 15.5%, while \(D\) remained invariant to numerical precision.
+It also supplies an exact alternative: inject boundary feedback
+\[
+-PDP^Tv
+\]
+while applying \(c\). The resulting field satisfies
+\[
+Av=c-PDP^Tv
+\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
+A^Tv=c.
+\]
+This would physically implement the adjoint.
+It is not a free actuator. The feedback needs calibrated gain, reference planes, bandwidth, noise control, voltage/current compliance, and dynamic stability. A static inverse identity does not qualify a delayed active controller.
+For a deliberately reversible skew-symmetric core, the simpler comparator is to reverse the core itself. Contemporary physical-backpropagation work already treats nonreciprocal systems with suitable known transformations and explicitly discusses their calibration and dynamic-range costs. arXiv
+Advance 2: physical synthesis reduces interior readout
+There is a better acquisition schedule than measuring every port-response column at every control site.
+Measure \(H\) at the ports, measure \(z_P\) at the ports, compute \(\beta\), then apply
+\[
+c+P\beta.
+\]
+The apparatus produces the adjoint field directly. Only that field and the original forward field need full control-site readout.
+For \(r\) input patterns sharing one linear operator, \(k\) nonreciprocal ports, and \(s\) sensed coordinates:
+Exact method, including forward acquisition	Settled source profiles	Scalar field readings
+Digital port completion	\(k+2r\)	\(s(k+2r)\)
+Port-only calibration, then physical synthesis	\(k+3r\)	\(k^2+kr+2rs\)
+Qualified physical core transposition	\(2r\)	\(2rs\)
+
+
+Physical synthesis trades more propagations for fewer interior readings. It does not eliminate interior sensing, source calibration, or potentially large correction-source amplitudes.
+These counts also expose an important restriction: the reuse across \(r\) inputs requires the same operator. When different inputs produce different nonlinear operating-point Jacobians, that reuse is invalid.
+3. A many-degree-of-freedom control test
+I constructed a larger synthetic problem rather than repeating the previous small gradient check.
+The plant has 144 nodes, 180 adjustable conductances, 100 sensed nodes, 44 unobserved nodes, and four declared nonreciprocal ports. Eight input patterns and sixteen output nodes define a response-shaping objective:
+\[
+J(p)=\frac{1}{2r}
+\left\|Q^TA(p)^{-1}B-T\right\|_F^2,
+\qquad r=8.
+\]
+Every controller receives the target \(T\), but not the configuration that generated it. The estimator receives only its permitted measurements and local control laws.
+For the declared design instance, 86 task-Jacobian singular values exceed \(0.1\%\) of the largest. This is a problem with many relevant control directions, not merely many parameters affecting one trivial output.
+Closed-loop comparison
+The benchmark uses a common 808-source-profile budget cap. Every proposed update is accepted only after evaluating the complete eight-input objective. Hyperparameters were selected on separate tuning seeds and tested on eight held-out systems.
+The stochastic method uses two-sided random directions and randomized input coding—not coordinate finite differences as a deliberately weak baseline. The tangent method also uses coded inputs.
+These closed-loop comparisons are noiseless. Noise and drift were tested separately.
+Method	Median remaining objective, \(J_{\rm final}/J_{\rm initial}\)	Source profiles	Scalar readings
+Digital port completion	3.77%	808	80,800
+Physically synthesized port completion	4.64%	792	46,944
+Qualified core transposition	1.19%	808	80,800
+Reciprocal approximation, with actual updates validated	1.45%	808	80,800
+Two-sided random-direction control	11.18%	808	12,928
+Random tangent-source control	6.99%	808	40,480
+
+
+The synthesized method cannot use its remaining sixteen profiles for a complete iteration.
+Several conclusions follow, but they require care.
+Port completion obtains a useful control direction efficiently in this supported model. At the profile budget shown, it outperforms the sampled stochastic baseline. However, digital completion uses 6.25 times as many scalar readings.
+The stochastic method also changes the controls much more often: approximately 538 configuration writes, versus 71 for digital completion. That can matter when switching controls is slow, costly, or disruptive.
+The tangent method needs up to 100 distributed injection sites in this construction. Its lower profile or read count does not grant that hardware for free.
+Most importantly, the table does not establish that exact port gradients are intrinsically worse than exact transposed-core gradients. They are the same gradients. The bounded tuning procedure selected different step sizes.
+The comparison without that optimizer confound
+I therefore repeated the three exact methods using the same update policy and the same forty attempted updates.
+Their objective trajectories agree to floating-point precision. All attain a median remaining objective of approximately 1.54%.
+Exact method, identical control decisions	Source profiles	Scalar readings	Core reversals
+Digital completion	808	80,800	0
+Physically synthesized completion	1,128	66,720	0
+Core transposition	648	64,800	80
+
+
+This is the robust result:
+The methods can deliver identical control information, while their physical acquisition costs differ substantially.
+
+For a serial-readout architecture, core transposition beats digital completion on acquisition time when
+\[
+\boxed{
+2t_{\rm flip}<k\,t_{\rm settle}+ks\,t_{\rm read},
+}
+\]
+after accounting for differential calibration and processing costs. A slow or unavailable reversal can make port completion preferable; a cheap qualified reversal removes that advantage.
+A separate equal-readout-budget test allowed the stochastic method approximately 5,048 profiles. Its median remaining objective fell to 2.81%, at the expense of roughly 3,470 configuration writes. That beats the initially tuned digital-completion run, but not the slower-step exact run above.
+Therefore neither the apparent ranking reversal nor the profile-count advantage proves total-cost superiority. The package retains the complete results, including this optimizer dependence, rather than selecting a favourable comparison.
+No measured seconds, joules, ADC power, controller power, or calibration lifetime have been assigned to these synthetic counts.
+4. Noise, drift and hidden structure
+Across thirty synthetic systems per condition, the digital reconstruction produced:
+Stress condition	Median relative gradient error	Maximum
+Supported, noiseless model	\(1.05\times10^{-15}\)	\(2.12\times10^{-15}\)
+0.1% profile-RMS field noise	0.32%	0.79%
+1% profile-RMS field noise	3.21%	7.96%
+1%-scale reciprocal drift over the acquisition block	1.85%	4.95%
+Undeclared skew coupling of amplitude 0.1	4.86%	19.34%
+Uncorrected 1%-scale port-source mixing	0.14%	1.22%
+
+
+These are chosen distributions in normalized circuit units, not measured apparatus tolerances. Correcting the source mixing using its independently known calibration restored numerical exactness.
+The good average behaviour cannot override an exact indistinguishability counterexample.
+Why small unobserved defects can matter
+Suppose a physically synthesized candidate satisfies
+\[
+(A+P\widehat D P^T)\widehat\lambda=c.
+\]
+Define the missed transpose defect
+\[
+R_{\rm miss}=A^T-A-P\widehat D P^T.
+\]
+Then exactly,
+\[
+\widehat\lambda-\lambda
+=A^{-T}R_{\rm miss}\widehat\lambda.
+\]
+For a candidate tangent source \(t\),
+\[
+\boxed{
+(\widehat\lambda-\lambda)^Tt
+=(A^{-1}t)^TR_{\rm miss}\widehat\lambda.
+}
+\]
+Thus “the hidden nonreciprocity is small” helps only when it has an independently justified bound and the relevant action margin is large enough. An arbitrarily small defect can reverse a nearly zero slope.
+Measurement calibration has an analogous problem. If the observed port response is
+\[
+\widetilde H=S_{\rm sensor}H M_{\rm source},
+\]
+its nonsymmetry can reflect source or sensor mismatch rather than physical nonreciprocity. Port locations alone do not supply these calibrations.
+5. Three exact ways the required control action remains unidentified
+A. Undeclared nonreciprocity
+The recovered counterexample uses
+\[
+A_\pm=I\pm e_2e_4^T,
+\]
+with ordinary source \(b=e_1\), objective source \(c=e_2\), and declared ports \(e_3,e_5\).
+Every field measured by the proposed protocol is identical in the two systems, even with complete state readout. Nevertheless, adding a conductance along \(v=e_1-e_4\) produces
+\[
+J_\pm(p)=\mp\frac{p}{1+2p}.
+\]
+The same action helps one system and harms the other. A probe at \(e_4\), or an actual control intervention, separates them. This violates the support assumption, not the identity.    RESEARCH_NOTE(20261015-020428)
+More generally, if the acquired fields are \(X=A^{-1}U\), then a perturbation satisfying
+\[
+\Delta A\,X=0
+\]
+can remain invisible to those acquisitions while changing an unprobed sensitivity. Additional measurements must address the relevant unobserved directions, or an independently valid structural restriction must exclude them.
+B. An inaccessible objective source—even with perfect reciprocity
+A new counterexample uses two symmetric positive-definite response matrices whose leading blocks are
+\[
+G_\pm=
+\begin{pmatrix}
+1&0.2&0\\
+0.2&1&\pm0.5\\
+0&\pm0.5&1
+\end{pmatrix},
+\]
+with two additional independent coordinates.
+Allow injections only at \(e_1,e_4,e_5\), while measuring the objective at \(e_2\). All available source responses are identical between the two systems, and both baseline objective values are \(0.2\).
+For a conductance between nodes \(1\) and \(3\), however, the derivatives are
+\[
+\boxed{+0.3\quad\text{and}\quad-0.7.}
+\]
+An objective detector at node \(2\) does not supply the missing source there.
+An \(e_2\) injection, a suitable tangent-source injection, or the actual conductance change supplies the missing information. Reciprocity alone does not.
+C. Unknown actuator response
+Two devices can have exactly the same operator at the measured setting but respond differently to the command:
+\[
+A_+(u)=A_0+u\,vv^T,\qquad
+A_-(u)=A_0-u\,vv^T.
+\]
+All fixed-setting source measurements agree at \(u=0\), but the command gradients have opposite signs. A sufficiently small range around a positive nominal conductance makes both changes admissible.
+Consequently, the desired gradient is
+\[
+\nabla_uJ
+=
+\left(\frac{\partial g}{\partial u}\right)^T\nabla_gJ,
+\]
+not automatically the conductance gradient. Cross-coupling, sign, gain and operating-point dependence in the actuator map must be acquired or guaranteed separately.
+No refinement of the port inverse identifies an actuator derivative that never entered the measurements.
+6. The alternatives already acquire much of the desired information
+Ordinary physical adjoints already operate through unknown reciprocal scattering hardware. Guillamon and colleagues’ microwave work is a relevant experimental baseline; its three-control hardware example must be distinguished from its larger numerical example. arXiv
+For nonreciprocal systems, the September 2026 Unifying Physical Backpropagation treatment supplies sufficient same-hardware transformations when an appropriate intertwiner is known and realizable. It explicitly accounts for recalibration and source-amplitude requirements; neither existence nor implementation of an arbitrary transformation is free. arXiv
+For a single proposed direction \(d\), the tangent-source route is especially important:
+\[
+t_d=b_p d-A_p[d]x,\qquad
+y=A^{-1}t_d,
+\]
+\[
+J'_d=F_p d+c^Ty.
+\]
+It requires neither reciprocity nor physical injection of \(c\). It does require the actual actuator derivative and access to the support of \(t_d\). A direct control trial avoids that derivative assumption but pays intervention and reset costs.
+Multiplexed and stochastic-gradient methods also avoid a complete exact gradient at every update. Their sample quality, perturbation cost and control-update timescales—not “two experiments per parameter”—are the appropriate comparisons. AIP Publishing
+Finally, the September 2026 physical-policy-gradient preprint describes a different stochastic acquisition route. It trades reciprocity for nondegenerate diffusion and transition-score information, including calibrated diffusion and parameter-response quantities. Its validation is simulation, and its trajectory budget is not equivalent to one inexpensive static measurement. It therefore expands the competing methods without supplying a free escape from acquisition requirements. arXiv
+7. A fundamentally different acquisition operation—and what it reveals
+After reaching the competitive boundary for port completion, I investigated changing boundary couplings rather than reconstructing an adjoint through the fixed operator.
+This has a concrete physical precedent: Virtual VNA 3.0 estimates a nonreciprocal multiport network using a few directly accessible ports, known individual terminations, and known coupled loads. Its experimental demonstration uses an eight-port network containing circulators, with four directly accessible ports and four load-connected ports. Its closed-form experiment uses nineteen load configurations—not nineteen scalar readings. This is an existing physical acquisition operation, not an Astra invention. arXiv
+Why coupled loads can reveal information that more ordinary measurements cannot
+The new illustrative test constructs two strictly dissipative nonreciprocal systems related by
+\[
+A_2=T A_1T^{-1},
+\qquad
+T=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,-1).
+\]
+Only ports \(1\) and \(2\) are directly driven and read. Every independent diagonal load on hidden ports \(3\) and \(4\) commutes with \(T\).
+Therefore the systems have identical external responses under every such independent-load configuration. This follows symbolically; one hundred random-load checks also returned zero difference.
+Now introduce a known bridge conductance
+\[
+p(e_3-e_4)(e_3-e_4)^T.
+\]
+That physical connection does not commute with the hidden transformation. In the constructed pair, its objective derivatives are
+\[
++0.04,\qquad -0.12.
+\]
+For the finite action \(p=0.1\), the objective changes are
+\[
++0.00333,\qquad -0.01000.
+\]
+The coupled intervention exposes exactly the information needed to distinguish the control action. Merely collecting more independent-load measurements would not.
+The converse is equally important
+When every allowed future control commutes with the hidden transformation, and the objective is externally observed, this internal ambiguity can be operationally irrelevant. Both models then predict the same outcomes for the available actions.
+That changes the interpretation of “closure”:
+The necessary acquisition is not whatever uniquely identifies the hidden system. It is whatever distinguishes alternatives that would change the admissible scientific decision.
+
+Sometimes a calibrated coupling is necessary. Sometimes identifying additional hidden parameters is unnecessary work.
+The physical coupled-load mechanism is already established prior art. The contribution here is the explicit action-level counterexample and its relevance to Astra’s acquisition criterion, not a priority claim for the mechanism.
+Final assessment
+The investigation separates four questions that should not be conflated.
+Is the identity correct under its assumptions?
+Yes. The reconstruction and its extensions survived the analytic and synthetic checks.
+Can the structural premise correspond to realistic hardware?
+Yes. Engineered reciprocal networks with a small nonreciprocal interface are credible, and closely matching microwave architectures exist. But their full source, sensing, actuator and parasitic-response requirements still need qualification.
+Has port completion demonstrated a meaningful total-cost advantage?
+No. It has conditional profile-count and control-preservation benefits. Physical synthesis improves its readout burden. Nevertheless, qualified core transposition can provide identical decisions more cheaply, stochastic methods trade fewer readings for more interventions, and calibrated multiport models already control closely relevant hardware.
+Does this establish the broader epistemic-closure hypothesis?
+No. It establishes a concrete failure mode: exact reconstruction can depend on information absent from the proposed measurements. It also shows why that is not the entire explanation—once the missing structure is supplied, novelty or competitive advantage may still disappear, and some hidden ambiguity need not be resolved at all.
+Port completion should therefore remain a conditional instrument technique, not be promoted as newly established scientific control power. Its plausible niche requires a real apparatus where control changes or core reversal are expensive, field acquisition is comparatively cheap, and all necessary sources and actuator responses are available in the same regime. No such matched-total-cost advantage was established here.

+# A concrete dependent kernel where every smooth product kernel fails
+
+Root construction, 15 October 2026. Independently reconstructed by the
+consequence investigator. Internal analytic proof; priority unresolved.
+
+Consider the constant-coefficient operation
+
+    Qp = p + partial_x² partial_y² p.
+
+Its real Laplace symbol is P(g)=1+g_x²g_y², strictly positive and already a
+sum of squares. Positivity of a polynomial symbol alone does not make its
+operation preserve positive densities. We construct one correlated density
+for which Qp is positive, while proving that no strictly positive smooth
+product density with all exponential moments can do so.
+
+## Explicit construction and all-point bound
+
+Set L=5, s=x²+y², t=1+s/L², ell=log t, and
+
+    h(s)=(L/2) sqrt(t) log t,
+    p(x,y)=Z^(-1) exp[-h(x²+y²)].
+
+This is a smooth radial probability density. Its Hessian potential has
+tangential eigenvalue (ell+2)/(2L sqrt(t)) and radial eigenvalue
+(2t+ell)/(2L t^(3/2)), both strictly positive. Thus p is strictly
+log-concave. Its potential divided by r tends to infinity, giving every
+exponential moment; all finite derivatives also have those weighted integrals.
+
+The derivatives of h are
+
+    h1=(ell+2)/(4L sqrt(t)),
+    h2=-ell/(8L³ t^(3/2)),
+    h3=(3ell-2)/(16L^5 t^(5/2)),
+    h4=(16-15ell)/(32L^7 t^(7/2)).
+
+Let
+
+    A2=h1²-h2,
+    A3=-h1³+3h1h2-h3,
+    A4=h1^4-6h1²h2+3h2²+4h1h3-h4.
+
+Differentiation gives the exact identity
+
+    (Qp)/p=1+4A2+8s A3+16x²y² A4.
+
+Here A2 is nonnegative. In A4 its first three displayed terms are
+nonnegative because h2<=0. Bound only the remaining negative terms.
+The elementary inequalities, for ell>=0 and t>=1, are
+
+    (ell+2)^3 exp(-ell/2) <= 216/e²,
+    ell(ell+2)exp(-ell) <= 2,
+    (3ell-2)_+ exp(-3ell/2) <= 1,
+    (t-1)²/t³ <= 4/27,
+    (ell+2)(2-3ell)_+ <= 4,
+    (t-1)²/t^(7/2) <= 1,
+    (16-15ell)_+ <= 16.
+
+Using s=L²(t-1) and 16x²y²<=4s² yields
+
+    (Qp)/p >= 1-B_L,
+    B_L=27/(e²L)+(3/2+4/27)/L²+5/(2L³).
+
+At L=5, B_L=0.8167364554036346...<1, so
+
+    Qp >= 0.1832635445963654... p > 0  everywhere.
+
+All derivatives decay sufficiently for integration by parts. Therefore
+integral Qp=integral p=1: Qp is another probability density. This is an
+explicit instance of the general Laplace-positive convolution criterion,
+without an unspecified scale or a remotely tested numerical tail.
+
+Integration over either coordinate annihilates the mixed derivative, so Qp
+has exactly the same two univariate marginals as p. Its mean and covariance
+are also unchanged, while integration by parts gives
+
+    E_Qp[X²Y²] = E_p[X²Y²] + 4.
+
+The operation therefore modifies dependence invisible to the coordinate
+laws and covariance. This is an exact identity for these normalized
+dimensionless variables, not a physical noise source already acquired.
+
+## Why every smooth product alternative fails
+
+Suppose p(x,y)=f(x)g(y), with f,g strictly positive C² probability densities
+having every exponential moment. A positive integrable C² function cannot
+be convex everywhere; choose y0 with g''(y0)<0. If Qp>=0 everywhere, then
+
+    f''(x)/f(x) <= K := -g(y0)/g''(y0)  for every x.
+
+Let H=Kf-f''>=0. For growing smooth compact cutoffs chi_R increasing to one,
+integration by parts gives, for each real a,
+
+    limit_R integral e^(ax) chi_R(x) H(x) dx
+       = (K-a²) integral e^(ax) f(x) dx.
+
+To justify the limit, move both derivatives onto exp(ax)chi_R.
+Cutoff derivative terms vanish by exponential integrability of f; no
+integrability of f'' is assumed. Every left integral is nonnegative, while
+the right side is negative when a²>K. This is a contradiction.
+
+In particular, for the isotropic Gaussian p_beta proportional to
+exp[-beta(x²+y²)/2],
+
+    (Qp_beta)(x,0)/p_beta(x,0)=1+beta²-beta³x²,
+
+which becomes negative for every beta>0. Increasing Gaussian width moves
+the failure into a more remote region and never removes it.
+
+Arbitrary nondegenerate correlated Gaussians fail as well. Write their
+precision matrix as A, put u=(A(z-mu))_1 and v=(A(z-mu))_2. Then
+
+    (Qp)/p = 1+u²v²-A22 u²-A11 v²-4A12 uv+A11 A22+2A12².
+
+Along v=0 with |u| tending to infinity, this tends to minus infinity.
+Invertibility of A guarantees that this line of points exists.
+
+## Meaning and limits
+
+Dependence changes exact positivity even for the elementary strictly positive
+scalar SOS symbol 1+g_x²g_y². The representation succeeds using correlated
+radial noise; every positive smooth product of all-exponential-moment factors
+fails. This is a scalar differential-operation example, distinct from the
+input's noncommuting quantum-observable example.
+
+It is not a positivity-preserving semigroup, an efficient sampler for every
+signed distribution, or a solution to the decision problem for polynomial
+positivity. The known general positive-multiplier/convolution literature is
+close; historical priority for this exact construction is UNKNOWN. Numerical
+checks verify calculus and finite instances, while the all-point conclusion
+rests on the displayed inequalities.

+# An implementable Pauli readout, and a cost of its exact projection law
+
+15 October 2026. Root derivation. This is an internal mathematical result,
+not a historical-priority claim or laboratory demonstration. The input's
+reciprocal-gamma kernel is user-supplied research, not a new result of this
+campaign. Ordinary covariant spin measurements are established prior art.
+
+## 1. Compile a radial positive qubit density without Fourier tomography
+
+Suppose a normalized qubit POVM has density
+
+    M(x) = u(r) I + v(r) n·sigma,  r=|x|, n=x/r,
+
+where u >= |v| and integral 4 pi r² u(r) dr = 1. Put
+
+    w(r)=4 pi r²u(r), a(r)=v(r)/u(r).
+
+Zero-u radii have zero probability and may be assigned any a. The following
+ideal sampling operation implements M on a supplied qubit state rho:
+
+1. Draw r from w independently of rho and n uniformly from the unit sphere.

+## 2. Explicit kernel and one-shot compiler
+
+Let
+\[
+f(r)=r p(r),\qquad I(r)=\int_{|r-1|}^{r+1}f(s)\,ds.
+\]
+The three-dimensional spherical-wave formula gives the scalar shell convolution
+\[
+g_\tau(r)=\frac{1}{2r}\int_{|r-\tau|}^{r+\tau}f(s)\,ds.
+\]
+For the Fourier convention in the supplied identity, \(u(r)=\partial_\tau g_\tau(r)|_{\tau=1}\) and \(v(r)=-\partial_r g_1(r)\). Thus, for \(0<r<1\),
+\[
+u(r)=\frac{f(r+1)-f(1-r)}{2r},\qquad
+v(r)=\frac{I(r)}{2r^2}-\frac{f(r+1)+f(1-r)}{2r},
+\]
+and, for \(r\ge1\),
+\[
+u(r)=\frac{f(r+1)+f(r-1)}{2r},\qquad
+v(r)=\frac{I(r)}{2r^2}-\frac{f(r+1)-f(r-1)}{2r}.
+\]
+These formulas reproduce the supplied identity
+\[
+u(r)-v(r)=\frac{f(r+1)}{r}-\frac{I(r)}{2r^2}.
+\]
+The value at \(r=0\) is immaterial to the continuous outcome law and can be set by the radial limit. Positivity of the supplied kernel means \(u(r)>0\) on its positive-mass support and
+\[
+a(r)=v(r)/u(r)\in[-1,1].
+\]
+Normalization gives the radial probability density \(w(r)=4\pi r^2u(r)\), with \(\int_0^\infty w(r)dr=1\).
+
+For input \(\rho=(I+s\cdot\sigma)/2\), run:

+1. Draw \(r\sim w\), independently of the state.
+2. Draw \(n\) uniformly on \(S^2\), and perform the projective measurement of \(n\cdot\sigma\), obtaining \(b\in\{\pm1\}\) with probability \((1+b\,s\cdot n)/2\).

+4. Return \(X=r\varepsilon n_0\).

+The two projective outcomes/axis pairs that yield a given \(n_0\) are \((n_0,+1)\) and \((-n_0,-1)\). Their total angular density is \((1+s\cdot n_0)/(4\pi)\). +convex on the whole line, and a nonzero nonnegative convex function is not
+integrable. If f g + f'' g'' >=0 everywhere, then at this y_0,
+
+    f''(x) <= K f(x) for all x,
+    K = -g(y_0)/g''(y_0) > 0.
+
+Set h=Kf-f''>=0. Transferring derivatives onto a compactly supported test
+function exp(t x)chi_R(x), exactly as in Section 2, gives
+
+    lim_R integral exp(t x)chi_R(x)h(x) dx
+       = (K-t^2) M_f(t).
+
+For |t|>sqrt(K) the right side is negative, whereas the left side is a limit
+of nonnegative numbers. This contradiction needs no integrability assumption
+on f'' and proves the claim.
+
+For centered isotropic Gaussian p_beta proportional to exp(-beta(x^2+y^2)/2),
+one can see the failure directly on y=0:
+
+    (p_beta + D_x^2D_y^2 p_beta)/p_beta
+        = 1+beta^2-beta^3 x^2.
+
+Every beta>0 therefore fails in sufficiently remote tails. The distinction
+is substantive even for a scalar sum-of-squares symbol: dependence between
+coordinates is necessary for this regularization class.
+
+In fact every nondegenerate Gaussian fails, including arbitrary correlation,
+covariance, and translation. Write
+
+    p proportional to exp(-(z-mu)^T A(z-mu)/2),      A positive definite,
+    u=(A(z-mu))_1,       v=(A(z-mu))_2.
+
+Then
+
+    D_x^2D_y^2 p / p
+      = u^2v^2 - A_22 u^2 - A_11 v^2 - 4A_12 u v
+        + A_11 A_22 + 2A_12^2.
+
+Because A is invertible, points with v=0 and arbitrarily large u exist.
+Along this line q/p=1+A_11 A_22+2A_12^2-A_22 u^2 tends to minus infinity.
+
+Every finite centered isotropic Gaussian mixture also fails. Along y=0,
+the component with smallest precision beta_* dominates, and the ratio is
+-beta_*^3 x^2+O(1). No claim is made here about arbitrary finite mixtures
+with nonradial means and covariance matrices.
+
+The product obstruction extends to every pair k,l>=1:
+
+    T=delta_0+D_x^(2k)D_y^(2l)delta_0,
+    L_T(u,v)=1+u^(2k)v^(2l)>0.
+
+The criterion supplies radial strictly log-concave regularization, but no
+positive sufficiently smooth product with all exponential moments works.
+If g^(2l)>=0 everywhere, testing against chi_R and moving derivatives to
+the cutoff gives integral g^(2l)=0 by monotone convergence, so g^(2l)=0.
+Then g is a polynomial, impossible for a positive integrable function.
+Thus g^(2l)<0 somewhere. At that point positivity forces f^(2k)<=Kf;
+the exponential-cutoff argument gives (K-t^(2k))M_f(t)>=0 for every t,
+which is impossible.
+
+For k=l=1, q=p+D_x^2D_y^2p preserves both one-variable
+marginals exactly, because integrating a second derivative in the other
+variable gives zero. It also satisfies
+
+    E_q[X^2Y^2] = E_p[X^2Y^2] + 4,
+
+while means, variances and E[XY] are unchanged. All these integrations are
+justified by the established absolute exponential moments of derivatives.
+
+6A. AN EXPLICIT REGULARIZER WITH A GLOBAL POSITIVITY MARGIN
+
+The following concrete density was proposed by the root investigator; every
+derivative, coefficient, and bound below was independently checked here.
+Set L=5 and
+
+    rho = sqrt(1+(x^2+y^2)/L^2),
+    p(x,y) = Z^(-1) exp(-L rho log(rho)).
+
+Then q=p+D_x^2D_y^2 p is a strictly positive probability density, and
+
+    q/p >= 1-B_L,
+    B_L = 27/(exp(2)L) + (3/2+4/27)/L^2 + 5/(2L^3) < 0.817.
+
+In particular the global lower bound is greater than 0.183. The density is
+radial, smooth, has negative-definite Hessian of its logarithm, and has all
+real exponential moments. No Gaussian and no strictly positive C^2 product
+density with all exponential moments can satisfy even q>=0 for this T.
+
+Verification. Put s=x^2+y^2, t=1+s/L^2, l=log(t), and
+
+    h(s)=(L/2)sqrt(t)log(t),             p=Z^(-1)exp(-h).
+
+The successive derivatives with respect to s are
+
+    h1=(l+2)/(4L sqrt(t)),
+    h2=-l/(8L^3 t^(3/2)),
+    h3=(3l-2)/(16L^5 t^(5/2)),
+    h4=(16-15l)/(32L^7 t^(7/2)).
+
+Write
+
+    A2=h1^2-h2,
+    A3=-h1^3+3h1 h2-h3,
+    A4=h1^4-6h1^2 h2+3h2^2+4h1 h3-h4.
+
+Direct differentiation gives
+
+    D_x^2D_y^2 p / p = 4A2 + 8s A3 + 16x^2y^2 A4.
+
+Since h1>0 and h2<=0, A2 and the first three terms of A4 are nonnegative.
+The negative contributions in 8s A3 are bounded, respectively, by
+
+    27/(exp(2)L),       3/(2L^2),       1/(2L^3).
+
+For the first use
+max_{l>=0}(l+2)^3 exp(-l/2)=216 exp(-2), attained at l=4.
+For the second use l(l+2)exp(-l)<=2. For the third use
+(3l-2)_+exp(-3l/2)<=1. The first inequality follows by differentiation
+or elementary comparison; the latter bound is deliberately loose.
+
+Since 16x^2y^2<=4s^2, the negative contribution from 4h1 h3 in A4 is
+at most 4/(27L^2): use
+
+    max_{t>=1}(t-1)^2/t^3=4/27,
+    (l+2)(2-3l)_+<=4.
+
+The negative contribution from -h4 is at most 2/L^3, by
+(t-1)^2/t^(7/2)<=1 and (16-15l)_+<=16. Adding these five bounds yields
+B_L as stated.
+
+The tangential and radial eigenvalues of Hess h(|x|^2) are, respectively,
+
+    2h1=(l+2)/(2L sqrt(t)) > 0,
+    2h1+4s h2=(2t+l)/(2L t^(3/2)) > 0.
+
+Finally L rho log(rho)/sqrt(s) tends to infinity, giving every exponential
+moment. Derivatives have at most polynomial/logarithmic factors times p,
+so integration by parts proves integral q=1 without boundary terms.
+
+More generally, for every Hermitian matrix polynomial P with P(0)=I, strict
+P(g)>0 for all real g is equivalent to the existence of a radial strictly
+log-concave probability p with all exponential moments for which P(-D)p is
+an everywhere positive-definite probability operator density. Here
+T=P(-D)delta_0, since <D^alpha delta_0,exp(g dot y)>=(-g)^alpha.
+
+7. STRICTNESS AND DEGENERATE NORMALIZATION
+
+Nonnegative L_T(g) is insufficient even in one scalar dimension. Take
+
+    T = delta_0 - 2 D^2 delta_0 + D^4 delta_0,
+    L_T(g)=(g^2-1)^2,     T(1)=1.
+
+Although L_T is nonnegative everywhere, it vanishes at g=1 and g=-1.
+Necessity proves that no smooth probability p with every exponential moment
+can make T*p merely nonnegative. Equivalently, no such p can satisfy
+
+    p-2p''+p'''' >=0 everywhere.
+
+For T(1)=A positive semidefinite but singular, the correct extension is:
+
+    T annihilates ker A on both matrix sides, and
+    L_T(g) restricted to ran A is positive definite for every real g.
+
+These conditions are necessary and sufficient for a positive semidefinite
+regularization of total mass A. Necessity: if v lies in ker A, positivity
+and zero integral force Q(x)v=0 for every x. Since the Fourier transform of
+p is continuous and nonzero near zero, Q=T*p implies T_hat(xi)v=0 on a
+real neighborhood. Compact support makes T_hat entire, hence T v=0.
+Apply the preceding theorem on ran A after congruence normalization by
+A^(-1/2). Sufficiency follows by that same reduction and embedding with
+zero on ker A. If A=0, necessarily T=0.
+
+Checking only L_T(g)>=0 is not enough when A is singular. The scalar
+T=D^2 delta_0 has L_T(g)=g^2>=0 and A=0 but T is nonzero, and p'' cannot
+be nonnegative for a probability density on the whole line.

+# Primary-literature comparison: Laplace-positive convolution regularization
+
+## Candidate and scope
+
+The candidate concerns a compactly supported finite-order Hermitian matrix distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^m$, normalized by $T(1)=I$. It asks whether strict positivity of its real Laplace transform
+
+$$L_T(g)=\langle T,e^{g\cdot y}\rangle\succ0\quad(g\in\mathbb R^m)$$
+
+is equivalent to existence of a smooth radial strictly log-concave probability density $p$, with every exponential moment, for which $p*T$ is pointwise positive definite. The proposed sufficiency permits arbitrarily small positive eigenvalue margins and chooses an adaptively slow unbounded radial log-slope. This is an overlap map, not a novelty finding.
+
+## Decisive scalar predecessor: Diamond–Essén
+
+H. G. Diamond and M. Essén, “Functions with non-negative convolutions,” *Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications* **63** (1978), no. 2, 463–489, [DOI 10.1016/0022-247X(78)90091-4](https://doi.org/10.1016/0022-247X(78)90091-4), is the closest scalar predecessor located. Katkova–Vishnyakova (below, p. 2) expressly describe it as investigating conditions on an input function $u$ that ensure existence of a nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ with $u*\mu\ge0$. This is directly about scalar convolution positivity and is therefore priority-critical.
+
+I could not verify Diamond–Essén’s theorem statement from the original paper. The ScienceDirect record labels it “Open archive,” but the publisher page and PDF route returned Cloudflare verification/403; Elsevier’s unkeyed text-mining endpoint returned minimized metadata only. No claim is made here about whether their criterion is exactly $L_u(x)>0$, whether it requires endpoint or quantitative margin conditions, or whether the result covers measures/distributions rather than functions. The proposed $L=BQ$ small-margin example therefore remains unclassified against Diamond–Essén. See [source receipts](SOURCE_RECEIPTS.md) for the access record. Reading the paper’s exact theorem is necessary before making a scalar priority claim.
+
+## Exact continuous scalar overlap: Katkova–Vishnyakova
+
+A. Katkova and A. Vishnyakova, “A Continual Analogue of a Theorem by M. Fekete and G. Pólya,” *Positivity* **5** (2001), 1–11, [DOI 10.1023/A:1009847605313](https://doi.org/10.1023/A:1009847605313), Theorems 1–2, give an exact scalar existence result. Their compact-support Theorem 2 assumes a real continuous function $u$ on $[a,b]$, with $u(a)>0$, $u(b)>0$, and bilateral Laplace transform $L_u(x)>0$ for every real $x$. Then there is $\varepsilon_0>0$ such that for each $0<\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$ there is $\lambda_\varepsilon>0$ for which, for every $\lambda\ge\lambda_\varepsilon$,
+
+$$L_u(x)e^{\lambda e^{\varepsilon x}}$$
+
+is the Laplace transform of a nonnegative function. The multiplier is the Laplace transform of the one-sided atomic measure $\mu_{\lambda,\varepsilon}$ on $\varepsilon\mathbb N$, with $\mu_{\lambda,\varepsilon}(\{\varepsilon k\})=\lambda^k/k!$; thus $u*\mu_{\lambda,\varepsilon}\ge0$. The hypothesis is pointwise strict transform positivity and includes no quantitative lower bound on $L_u$ at infinity. The proof handles tails through the positive endpoint values and uses compact-set positivity in the middle. So a global transform margin is not required within this endpoint class.
+
+This does not settle the candidate. A smooth compactly supported density extended by zero has zero endpoint values at the boundary of its support, so Theorem 2 does not apply directly. Its output is nonnegative and obtained with a one-sided atomic, $u$-dependent choice of $\lambda$ and small $\varepsilon$; it is not a single smooth radial probability kernel and does not assert pointwise strict positivity on all of $\mathbb R^m$. The paper’s Theorem 1 extends the input to a continuous half-line function with integrable exponential tails, nonnegative outside a bounded interval, positive at some point on each tail, and $L_u(x)>0$ for all real $x$. It still uses the same atomic multiplier.
+
+The authors explicitly distinguish their “standard” multiplier, whose form is independent of $u$, from Diamond–Essén’s more general existence question; they also give an example showing their fixed lattice multiplier need not work for a signed measure even when its bilateral Laplace transform is positive and the measure is positive near its support endpoints (Remark, pp. 10–11). That example refutes universal applicability of their particular multiplier, not existence of an arbitrary positive convolution measure.
+
+## Poincaré–Pólya and Handelman: finite-support coefficient positivity
+
+Katkova–Vishnyakova state the Fekete–Pólya theorem: if a real polynomial $f(u)$ is strictly positive for $u\ge0$, then for all sufficiently large $\lambda$, $e^{\lambda u}f(u)$ has nonnegative Taylor coefficients. Interpreting $f(u)=\sum_k a_k u^k$ as the Laplace transform of a finitely supported signed measure on $\mathbb N$ identifies this with a discrete convolution/coefficient result. It has finite support and a discrete Poisson-type multiplier, rather than a smooth radial kernel on Euclidean space.
+
+For multivariate finite support, D. Handelman, “Deciding eventual positivity of polynomials,” *Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems* **6** (1986), 57–79, [DOI 10.1017/S0143385700003291](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0143385700003291), gives the sharp lattice comparison. In the easier multiplier problem in §I (pp. 57–58), a Laurent polynomial $f$ admits a Laurent polynomial $Q$ with nonnegative coefficients and $Qf$ coefficientwise nonnegative iff every face polynomial $f_F$ of its Newton polytope, including $f$ itself, is strictly positive on the positive orthant. The eventual-power Theorem A combines strict positivity for dominant strata of the full support of $f$ with recursive proper-face coefficient conditions; Theorem B gives a criterion through strict positivity on the appropriate dominant strata for the relative faces of $\operatorname{supp}P$. These are finite lattice/coefficient criteria, not all-real-parameter Laplace criteria or convolution by a smooth density. Handelman’s introduction records the historical scope: Poincaré handled one variable; Meissner and Pólya treated cases with standard hypercube/simplex Newton polyhedra.
+
+D. Handelman, “Representing polynomials by positive linear functions on compact convex polyhedra,” *Pacific Journal of Mathematics* **132** (1988), 35–62, [DOI 10.2140/pjm.1988.132.35](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.1988.132.35), Theorem 1.3 (p. 39), proves that a polynomial strictly positive on a compact full-dimensional polyhedron defined by affine inequalities $\beta_i\ge0$ is a finite linear combination, with nonnegative coefficients, of products of the defining $\beta_i$. This is a compact-domain algebraic positivity certificate, not a Laplace-transform or convolution theorem.
+
+## Matrix and operator polynomial analogues
+
+Lê and Dư, “Handelman’s Positivstellensatz for polynomial matrices positive definite on polyhedra,” *Positivity* **22** (2018), 449–460, [DOI 10.1007/s11117-017-0520-y](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11117-017-0520-y), Theorems 2.1 and 3.1, prove a matrix-polynomial extension on compact polyhedra. On a simplex, if a symmetric polynomial matrix $F$ has degree $d>0$ and a uniform margin $F\succeq\lambda I$ there, their Bernstein–Bézier coefficient bound gives positive-definite constant matrix coefficients in the Handelman representation for integers
+
+$$N>\frac{d(d-1)}{2}\frac{C}{\lambda}-d,$$
+
+where $C$ is the stated coefficient norm of the homogeneous lift. The polyhedron theorem reduces to a lifted simplex and also assumes a positive margin on that compact simplex. This gives a finite-dimensional matrix positivity analogue, but its explicit bound depends on a uniform compact-domain margin; it does not concern matrix distributions, Laplace multipliers, or a radial kernel.
+
+J. Cimprič and A. Zalar, “Moment problems for operator polynomials,” *Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications* **401** (2013), 307–316, [DOI 10.1016/j.jmaa.2012.12.027](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jmaa.2012.12.027), Theorems 3–5, extend Haviland-type representing-measure results to operator-polynomial maps and give compact archimedean/Schmüdgen-type results. For operator-valued output on a general closed set, their Theorem 4 assumes complete positivity; for compact sets, their Remark 6 says positivity suffices. Their §5 example shows that the archimedeanity and strict-positivity certificate assertions of the finite-dimensional matrix Theorem 6 fail for operator polynomials; they leave the corresponding representing-measure assertion open. These are moment representation and semialgebraic positivity results; they do not give a convolution regularizer or Laplace-positive-distribution criterion.
+
+## Comparison and priority limit
+
+The necessary implication for the candidate is elementary whenever the transforms exist: $L_{p*T}(g)=L_p(g)L_T(g)$, and $L_p(g)>0$ for a probability density $p>0$. Hence $p*T\succ0$ implies $L_T(g)\succ0$.
+
+The accessible sources establish close scalar overlap with no global transform-margin hypothesis for inputs positive at their support endpoints, and extensive finite-support scalar, matrix, and operator polynomial analogues. They do not state the full proposed combination of arbitrary compactly supported finite-order Hermitian matrix distributions on $\mathbb R^m$, pointwise positive transform with margins allowed to decay arbitrarily, and one smooth radial strictly log-concave probability kernel giving pointwise strict output. Diamond–Essén is the decisive scalar source, and its exact theorem remains unread here. Therefore this comparison supports neither a novelty claim nor a claim that the scalar full criterion is preexisting.
