+# A scalar-convolution criterion for compact distributions with values in an ordered space
+
+Status: internally reconstructed theorem candidate, 2026-10-15. The argument below is mathematical work, not a claim of historical priority, independent review, formal verification, or exceptional practical capability.
+
+## 1. Result and scope
+
+The supplied quantum-observable candidate suggests retaining a positive real exponential tilt and perturbing only its logarithmic remainder. The extension here removes its quantitative exponential lower-bound assumption and gives an exact criterion for arbitrary compact distributions.
+
+Let \(E\) be a real Banach space and \(C\subsetneq E\) a closed convex cone with nonempty interior. Pointedness is not needed. Write \(u\preceq_C v\) when \(v-u\in C\). Fix \(e\in\operatorname{int}C\). Let
+\[
+T:C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^m)\longrightarrow E
+\]
+be a continuous linear distribution with compact support and \(T(1)=e\). Compact support makes evaluation on every smooth function meaningful by inserting a cutoff equal to one near the support. Its real Laplace transform is
+\[
+\mathcal L_T(g)=T_y(e^{g\cdot y}),\qquad g\in\mathbb R^m.
+\]
+
+Define the admissible scalar class
+\[
+\mathscr E=\left\{p\in C^\infty(\mathbb R^m):
+\int_{\mathbb R^m}e^{a|x|}|\partial^\alpha p(x)|\,dx<\infty
+\ \text{for every }a\ge0,\ \alpha\right\}.
+\tag{1}
+\]
+
+Call a distribution \(S\) \(C\)-positive if \(S(\phi)\in C\) for every nonnegative real \(\phi\in C_c^\infty\). **Theorem.** The following conditions are equivalent.
+
+1. \(\mathcal L_T(g)\in\operatorname{int}C\) for every real \(g\).
+2. There is a scalar probability measure \(\nu\) satisfying \(\int e^{a|z|}\nu(dz)<\infty\) for every \(a\ge0\), such that \(T*\nu\) is a \(C\)-positive distribution.
+3. There is a strictly positive probability density \(p\in\mathscr E\) such that \(M=T*p\) takes values in \(C\).
+
+Moreover, when condition 1 holds, for every \(0<\varepsilon<1\) one can choose \(p\) smooth, radial, and strictly log-concave, with
+\[
+(1-\varepsilon)p(x)\mathcal L_T(\nabla V(x))
+\preceq_C M(x)
+\preceq_C
+(1+\varepsilon)p(x)\mathcal L_T(\nabla V(x)),
+\qquad p=Z^{-1}e^{-V}.
+\tag{2}
+\]
+Thus \(M(x)\in\operatorname{int}C\) at every \(x\), and
+\[
+\int_{\mathbb R^m}M(x)\,dx=e.
+\tag{3}
+\]
+The output and all its derivatives are integrable in norm after multiplication by every \(e^{a|x|}\).
+
+For \(E=\operatorname{Herm}_d\) and \(C\) the positive-semidefinite cone, the criterion is exactly
+\[
+\mathcal L_T(g)\succ0\quad\text{for all }g\in\mathbb R^m.
+\]
+For self-adjoint elements of a unital \(C^*\)-algebra, interior positivity means positive invertibility, with a separate positive lower bound permitted at each \(g\). The proof applies in that setting too.
+
+There is no prescribed decay rate for the positivity margin. In particular, no constants \(\eta,b>0\) satisfying
+\(\mathcal L_T(g)\succeq\eta e^{-b|g|}I\) are assumed. Section 7 constructs a compact smooth scalar density with strictly positive Laplace transform for which every such bound fails.
+
+## 2. Compact distributions preserve the admissible class
+
+Choose \(R_1>0\), a cutoff \(\chi\in C_c^\infty(B_{R_1})\) equal to one near the support of \(T\), a nonnegative integer \(N\), and \(C_T<\infty\) so that
+\[
+\|T(h)\|
+\le C_T\max_{|\alpha|\le N}\sup_{B_{R_1}}|\partial^\alpha h|.
+\tag{4}
+\]
+Cutoff differentiation is absorbed into \(C_T\). Such data exist by continuity of a compactly supported distribution.
+
+For completeness, a local supremum can be bounded by local integrals of finitely many derivatives. If \(h\) is compactly supported, repeated use of the fundamental theorem of calculus in the \(m\) coordinate directions gives
+\[
+|h(y)|\le\int_{\mathbb R^m}
+|\partial_1\cdots\partial_m h(u)|\,du.
+\]
+Apply this to derivatives of \(\chi(y)p(x-y)\). Equation (4) then gives
+\[
+\|M(x)\|
+\le C\sum_{|\beta|\le N+m}
+\int_{B_{R_1}}|\partial^\beta p(x-y)|\,dy,
+\tag{5}
+\]
+after increasing the finite constant and derivative index if the cutoff requires it. The same estimate applies to every derivative of \(M\).
+
+Since \(|x|\le|x-y|+R_1\) on the integral,
+\[
+\int e^{a|x|}\|M(x)\|\,dx
+\le C_a\sum_{|\beta|\le N+m}
+\int e^{a|z|}|\partial^\beta p(z)|\,dz<\infty.
+\tag{6}
+\]
+This justifies all following integrals in Banach norm and the interchange of \(T\) with the integrals. In particular,
+\[
+\int M(x)\,dx=T(1)=e,
+\tag{7}
+\]
+and
+\[
+\int e^{g\cdot x}M(x)\,dx
+=\left(\int e^{g\cdot x}p(x)\,dx\right)\mathcal L_T(g).
+\tag{8}
+\]
+
+The derivative condition in (1) is material. Finite exponential moments of \(p\) alone would not justify applying an arbitrary finite-order distribution and interchanging these integrals.
+
+## 3. Necessity for any scalar probability measure
+
+This proof does not assume derivatives, or even a density, for the input noise. Let \(\nu\) be as in condition 2 and write \(S=T*\nu\). Distributional convolution is well-defined because \(T\) is compactly supported:
+\[
+S(\phi)=T_y\left(\int\phi(y+z)\,\nu(dz)\right).
+\]
+Choose a smooth radial cutoff \(\chi\), equal to one on \(B_1\), zero outside \(B_2\), with \(0\le\chi\le1\) and radial profile nonincreasing. Put \(\chi_R(x)=\chi(x/R)\). For a fixed real \(g\), define
+\[
+h_{R,g}(y)=\int e^{g\cdot(y+z)}\chi_R(y+z)\,\nu(dz).
+\]
+On every fixed compact \(y\)-set,
+\[
+h_{R,g}\longrightarrow
+\left(\int e^{g\cdot z}\nu(dz)\right)e^{g\cdot y}
+\quad\text{in }C^N.
+\tag{9a}
+\]
+Indeed, differentiating under the integral gives sums of
+\[
+e^{g\cdot(y+z)}g^{\alpha-\beta}
+R^{-|\beta|}(\partial^\beta\chi)((y+z)/R).
+\]
+For \(\beta=0\), the error on \(|y|\le R_1\) is bounded by a constant times
+\(\int_{|z|>R-R_1}e^{g\cdot z}\nu(dz)\), which tends to zero. For \(|\beta|>0\), the uniform bound contains \(R^{-|\beta|}\int e^{g\cdot z}\nu(dz)\) and also tends to zero. Thus (4) proves the norm limit
+\[
+S(e^{g\cdot x}\chi_R(x))
+\longrightarrow
+\left(\int e^{g\cdot z}\nu(dz)\right)\mathcal L_T(g).
+\tag{9b}
+\]
+
+At \(g=0\), \(Q_R:=S(\chi_R)\to T(1)=e\) in norm. Choose finite \(A\) with \(Q_A\in\operatorname{int}C\).
+For \(R\ge2A\),
+\[
+e^{g\cdot x}\chi_R(x)
+-e^{-2A|g|}\chi_A(x)\ge0
+\quad\text{at every }x.
+\]
+Hence \(C\)-positivity gives
+\[
+S(e^{g\cdot x}\chi_R(x))
+-e^{-2A|g|}Q_A\in C.
+\]
+Taking the norm limit (9b) and using closedness of \(C\) shows that the limit is the sum of an interior cone element and a cone element, so it is interior. The scalar Laplace transform of \(\nu\) is finite and strictly positive; therefore \(\mathcal L_T(g)\in\operatorname{int}C\).
+
+In finite matrix dimension, \(C\)-positive distributions are positive matrix measures, and the growing cutoffs also establish their normalization and finite exponential moments. The cutoff proof itself works for Banach cone values and avoids assuming that a weakly normalized arbitrary POVM is norm tight.
+
+Condition 3 implies condition 2 immediately. Section 6 proves condition 1 implies condition 3, completing all three equivalences.
+
+## 4. An explicit slow-slope lemma
+
+The main construction is not an unspecified instruction to choose a function slowly enough.
+
+Let \(G:[1,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\) be any finite, nondecreasing function. Fix once and for all a smooth nondecreasing step
+\[
+\theta(s)=0\quad(s\le0),\qquad
+\theta(s)=1\quad(s\ge1).
+\]
+For example, on \(0<s<1\), take
+\[
+\theta(s)=
+\frac{e^{-1/s}}{e^{-1/s}+e^{-1/(1-s)}}.
+\]
+Choose the thresholds inductively:
+\[
+S_1=\max\{2,\ 2\log G(2)\},
+\]
+\[
+S_{n+1}
+=\max\{S_n+2,\ 2(n+1),\ 2\log G(n+2)\}.
+\tag{9}
+\]
+Define, for \(s\ge0\),
+\[
+q(s)=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\theta(s-S_n).
+\tag{10}
+\]
+The sum is locally finite.
+
+Then:
+
+- \(q\) is smooth and nondecreasing, \(q\ge1\), and \(q(s)\to\infty\).
+- \(q(s)\le1+s/2\).
+- For every \(k\ge1\), \(\sup_s|q^{(k)}(s)|\le\|\theta^{(k)}\|_\infty\), because the transition intervals are disjoint.
+- If \(|s-t|\le1\) and \(s,t\ge0\), then \(q(t)\le q(s)+1\).
+- With \(C_G=\max\{1,G(1)\}\),
+\[
+G(q(s))\le C_G e^{s/2}.
+\tag{11}
+\]
+
+To check the last assertion, before \(S_1\) one has \(q=1\). Otherwise let \(n\) be the latest activated threshold. Throughout its transition and the succeeding plateau, \(q(s)\le n+1\), and
+\[
+G(q(s))\le G(n+1)\le e^{S_n/2}\le e^{s/2}.
+\]
+Every threshold is finite; no restriction is imposed on how rapidly the sequence grows.
+
+One can impose any additional finite lower bounds on \(S_n\), for example to make \(q\) grow beneath a specified unbounded increasing envelope. All conclusions remain true.
+
+## 5. A strictly convex radial potential with controlled jets
+
+For \(z\in\mathbb R^m\), put
+\[
+\rho(z)=\sqrt{1+|z|^2},\qquad s(z)=\log\rho(z),
+\]
+\[
+H(u)=\int_1^u q(\log v)\,dv,\qquad
+f(z)=H(\rho(z)).
+\tag{12}
+\]
+The function \(f\) is smooth and radial. Since \(q>0\) and \(q'\ge0\),
+\[
+\nabla f(z)=q(s)\frac z\rho,
+\tag{13}
+\]
+\[
+D^2f(z)
+=q(s)D^2\rho(z)
++\frac{q'(s)}{\rho}\nabla\rho(z)\otimes\nabla\rho(z)\succ0.
+\tag{14}
+\]
+Here \(D^2\rho=\rho^{-1}I-\rho^{-3}zz^\top\), whose radial eigenvalue is \(\rho^{-3}>0\). Thus strict convexity holds even on the plateaus of \(q\).
+
+For every \(k\ge2\), there is a finite \(C_k\), depending only on \(m,k,\theta\), such that
+\[
+\|D^k f(z)\|\le C_k q(s)\rho^{1-k}.
+\tag{15}
+\]
+Indeed, \(D^j\rho=O_j(\rho^{1-j})\). For \(\ell\ge2\),
+\[
+H^{(\ell)}(u)
+=u^{1-\ell}P_\ell(q'(\log u),\ldots,q^{(\ell-1)}(\log u)),
+\]
+where \(P_\ell\) is a fixed linear combination. The bounded derivatives of \(q\), and \(q\ge1\), give
+\(|H^{(\ell)}(u)|\le C_\ell q(\log u)u^{1-\ell}\).
+The chain rule for \(H\circ\rho\) gives (15), term by term.
+
+Also,
+\[
+\frac{f(z)}{|z|}\longrightarrow\infty.
+\tag{16}
+\]
+For large \(\rho\), the integral defining \(H\) over \([\rho/2,\rho]\) is at least
+\((\rho/2)q(\log(\rho/2))\), and this divided by \(|z|\) tends to infinity.
+
+For \(L\ge1\), let
+\[
+V_L(x)=L f(x/L),\qquad
+p_L(x)=Z_L^{-1}e^{-V_L(x)}.
+\tag{17}
+\]
+Equation (16) makes \(0<Z_L<\infty\) and gives every exponential moment.
+Equations (13), (15), and \(q(s)\le1+s/2\) show, for every multi-index \(\alpha\),
+\[
+|\partial^\alpha p_L(x)|
+\le C_{\alpha,L}\,p_L(x)
+\bigl(1+\log\sqrt{1+|x/L|^2}\bigr)^{|\alpha|}.
+\tag{18}
+\]
+Thus \(p_L\in\mathscr E\). It is radial, smooth, strictly positive, and strictly log-concave.
+
+## 6. Sufficiency and the global error bound
+
+For a point \(w\in\operatorname{int}C\), define its interior radius
+\[
+d_C(w)=\operatorname{dist}(w,E\setminus C).
+\]
+It is finite, strictly positive, and 1-Lipschitz on the interior. Define
+\[
+\mu(t)=\min_{|g|\le t}d_C(\mathcal L_T(g))>0.
+\tag{19}
+\]
+The minimum exists because the real \(g\)-ball is compact and the transform is continuous. The function \(\mu\) is nonincreasing.
+
+Use the slow-slope lemma with
+\[
+G(t)=\max\left\{1,\
+\frac{e^{R_1t}(1+t)^{N+1}}{\mu(t)}\right\},
+\qquad t\ge1.
+\tag{20}
+\]
+This is finite and nondecreasing.
+
+Fix \(x\), let \(z=x/L\), \(\rho=\rho(z)\), \(s=\log\rho\), and
+\[
+g=\nabla V_L(x)=\nabla f(z).
+\]
+For \(|y|\le R_1\), define the exact logarithmic remainder
+\[
+F_x(y)=V_L(x-y)-V_L(x)+g\cdot y.
+\tag{21}
+\]
+Assume \(L\ge\max\{1,R_1\}\). The function \(\log\rho\) is 1-Lipschitz, so at \(z-y/L\) its value differs from \(s\) by at most one; the corresponding \(\rho\)'s differ by factors at most \(e\), and the corresponding \(q\)'s differ by at most one.
+
+Taylor's integral remainder for orders zero and one, followed by (15) for higher orders, gives
+\[
+\max_{|\alpha|\le N}\sup_{|y|\le R_1}
+|\partial_y^\alpha F_x(y)|
+\le \frac{C_0}{L}\frac{q(s)+1}{\rho}.
+\tag{22}
+\]
+If \(N<2\), the same argument still uses the available second derivative of \(V_L\). For \(k\ge2\), the scaling is
+\[
+\|D^kV_L(x-y)\|
+\le C_k L^{1-k}(q(s)+1)\rho^{1-k}
+\le\frac{C_k}{L}\frac{q(s)+1}{\rho}.
+\]
+The constants in (22) depend only on the fixed seminorm data, \(m,N,\theta\), not on \(x,L\), or the threshold locations.
+
+Because \(q(s)\le1+s/2\), \((q(s)+1)e^{-s}\) is bounded. Increasing \(L\) makes the left side of (22) at most one for all \(x\). The product and chain rules therefore imply
+\[
+\|e^{-F_x}-1\|_{C^N(B_{R_1})}
+\le\frac{C_1}{L}\frac{q(s)+1}{\rho}.
+\tag{23}
+\]
+
+The identity
+\[
+p_L(x-y)
+=p_L(x)e^{g\cdot y}e^{-F_x(y)}
+\tag{24}
+\]
+is exact. Hence
+\[
+\frac{M_L(x)}{p_L(x)}
+=\mathcal L_T(g)+E_x,
+\qquad
+E_x=T_y\!\left(e^{g\cdot y}(e^{-F_x(y)}-1)\right).
+\tag{25}
+\]
+Using (4), (23), and \(|g|\le q(s)\), we obtain
+\[
+\|E_x\|
+\le\frac{C_2}{L}
+e^{R_1q(s)}(1+q(s))^{N+1}e^{-s}.
+\tag{26}
+\]
+Divide by \(\mu(q(s))\) and use (11), (20):
+\[
+\frac{\|E_x\|}{\mu(q(s))}
+\le\frac{C_2C_G}{L}e^{-s/2}
+\le\frac{C_2C_G}{L}.
+\tag{27}
+\]
+Take \(L\) large enough to meet the previous finite lower bounds and
+\[
+L\ge C_2C_G/\varepsilon.
+\tag{28}
+\]
+Since \(|g|\le q(s)\),
+\[
+\|E_x\|
+\le\varepsilon\,\mu(q(s))
+\le\varepsilon\,d_C(\mathcal L_T(g)).
+\]
+The ball of radius \(\varepsilon d_C(\mathcal L_T(g))\) centered at
+\(\varepsilon\mathcal L_T(g)\) lies in \(C\), by homogeneity of the cone.
+Therefore
+\[
+-\varepsilon\mathcal L_T(g)
+\preceq_C E_x
+\preceq_C\varepsilon\mathcal L_T(g).
+\]
+This is (2). Since \(1-\varepsilon>0\), its lower bound is interior, proving pointwise strict positivity. Equations (3) and the weighted norm integrability follow from Section 2.
+
+This completes the three-way equivalence.
+
+## 7. The missing exponential margin is a real extension
+
+Here is an explicit compact smooth real scalar density \(t\) with
+\(\int t=1\), strictly positive real Laplace transform, and no exponential lower bound. Positivity of \(t\) itself is neither asserted nor needed.
+
+Let
+\[
+A=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}j^{-2}=\pi^2/6,\qquad
+B(z)=\prod_{j=1}^{\infty}
+\frac{\sinh(z/j^2)}{z/j^2}.
+\tag{29}
+\]
+Each factor is the Laplace transform of a uniform probability law on
+\([-j^{-2},j^{-2}]\). The product is the Laplace transform of their independent, absolutely convergent sum, supported in \([-A,A]\). It is entire, \(B(0)=1\), and \(B(s)>0\) for real \(s\).
+
+For any complex \(w\),
+\[
+\left|\frac{\sinh w}{w}\right|
+\le e^{|\operatorname{Re}w|}
+\min\{1,|w|^{-1}\}.
+\tag{30}
+\]
+The first bound follows from the integral representation of \(\sinh w/w\); the second uses
+\(|\sinh(u+iv)|^2=\sinh^2u+\sin^2v\le\cosh^2u\).
+For \(n=\lfloor\sqrt{|z|}/2\rfloor\), the first \(n\) minimum factors in (30) are at most \(1/4\). Thus
+\[
+|B(z)|\le C\exp\{A|\operatorname{Re}z|-c\sqrt{|z|}\}.
+\tag{31}
+\]
+This is a full complex-plane estimate, not just a bound on the imaginary axis.
+
+Let \(r_n=2^{2^n}\), \(H_n=e^{r_n^2}\), \(\delta_n=e^{-H_n}\), and
+\[
+Q(z)=\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}
+\frac{(z-r_n)^2+\delta_n^2}{r_n^2+\delta_n^2}.
+\tag{32}
+\]
+The product converges uniformly on compact subsets because
+\(\sum_n r_n^{-1}<\infty\). Each factor is strictly positive for real \(z\), its deviations from one are summable at every fixed real \(z\), and no factor vanishes there. Therefore \(Q(s)>0\) for real \(s\), with \(Q(0)=1\).
+
+The elementary bound
+\[
+\left|
+\frac{(z-r_n)^2+\delta_n^2}{r_n^2+\delta_n^2}
+\right|
+\le (1+|z|/r_n)^2
+\]
+and \(r_n\ge2^n\) give
+\[
+|Q(z)|\le\exp\{C\log^2(2+|z|)\}.
+\tag{33}
+\]
+To see this, split the logarithmic sum at
+\(n=\lceil\log_2(2+|z|)\rceil\); the initial part is \(O(\log^2(2+|z|))\), and the remaining geometric tail is bounded.
+
+Set \(L(z)=B(z)Q(z)\). Combining (31)–(33), for every integer \(k\ge0\),
+\[
+|L(z)|\le C_k(1+|z|)^{-k}
+e^{A|\operatorname{Re}z|}.
+\tag{34}
+\]
+The standard smooth Paley–Wiener theorem, applied to \(L(i\xi)\), now yields a real \(t\in C_c^\infty([-A,A])\) whose bilateral Laplace transform is \(L\). Reality follows from \(L(\overline z)=\overline{L(z)}\). One also has \(L(0)=1\) and \(L(s)>0\) for every real \(s\).
+
+At \(s=r_n\), the \(n\)-th factor in (32) is
+\(\delta_n^2/(r_n^2+\delta_n^2)\). Apply (33)'s product estimate to the other factors and \(B(r_n)\le e^{Ar_n}\):
+\[
+0<L(r_n)
+\le\exp\{-2H_n+Ar_n+C\log^2(2+r_n)\}
+\le e^{-H_n}
+\tag{35}
+\]
+for all sufficiently large \(n\).
+Consequently there are no \(\eta,b>0\) with
+\(L(s)\ge\eta e^{-b|s|}\) for every real \(s\).
+
+The theorem above still produces a radial—in one dimension, even—smooth strictly log-concave probability density \(p\in\mathscr E\) with \(t*p>0\) everywhere. This example separates the new hypothesis from the exponential-margin sufficient condition in the supplied attachment.
+
+In fact, no scalar noise density bounded above in both tails by
+\[
+p(x)\le C e^{-c|x|\log|x|}
+\quad\text{for any fixed }c>0
+\tag{35a}
+\]
+can regularize this particular \(t\).
+To prove this, suppose \(\nu\) is any probability noise with all exponential moments and \(M=t*\nu\) is positive. The cutoff proof gives
+\(\mathcal L_M(s)=\mathcal L_\nu(s)L(s)\), and \(M\) has total mass one. Some finite interval \([-D,D]\) carries at least half its mass, so
+\[
+\mathcal L_M(s)\ge\tfrac12 e^{-D s}\qquad(s\ge0).
+\]
+With \(K_\nu=\log\mathcal L_\nu\), (35) implies
+\[
+K_\nu(r_n)\ge H_n-Dr_n-\log2
+=e^{r_n^2}-O(r_n).
+\tag{35b}
+\]
+On the other hand, (35a) implies, for any \(0<c'<c\),
+\[
+K_\nu(s)\le C_1+C_2e^{s/c'}\qquad(s\ge0).
+\tag{35c}
+\]
+Indeed, optimize \(sr-c'r\log r\) to obtain
+\(\sup_{r>0}(sr-c'r\log r)=c'e^{s/c'-1}\), and integrate the remaining factor
+\(e^{-(c-c')r\log r}\); a bounded central interval contributes only \(e^{O(s)}\).
+Equations (35b)–(35c) contradict each other.
+Thus the whole fixed positive-coefficient \(r\log r\) upper-tail class can be insufficient for general compact smooth Laplace-positive inputs, although it suffices under the supplied quantum exponential-margin hypotheses.
+
+## 8. Singular matrix masses: the exact extension
+
+For a compact \(\operatorname{Herm}_d\)-valued distribution without the normalization \(T(1)=I\), there is an admissible positive probability \(p\) with \(T*p\succeq0\) if and only if
+
+1. \(\mathcal L_T(g)\succeq0\) for every real \(g\); and
+2. \(\ker\mathcal L_T(g)\) is independent of \(g\).
+
+The zero distribution is included.
+
+For necessity with an admissible smooth density, \(Q=T(1)=\int M\succeq0\). For \(v\in\ker Q\), the continuous nonnegative scalar function \(v^*M(x)v\) has integral zero and vanishes everywhere. Positivity then gives \(M(x)v=0\). For \(v\notin\ker Q\), its positive total mass makes its exponentially weighted integral strictly positive. Equation (8) therefore yields
+\(\ker\mathcal L_T(g)=\ker Q\).
+For an arbitrary probability measure with all exponential moments, the cutoff argument of Section 3 gives the same moment identity and normalization of the positive output matrix measure, so the identical kernel argument applies.
+
+For sufficiency, let \(K\) be the fixed kernel. Each Laplace transform annihilates \(K\), so every corresponding component of the distribution vanishes: the entire Laplace transform is zero on \(\mathbb R^m\), hence identically zero by iterating the one-variable identity theorem; uniqueness of the Fourier transform then applies. Compress to \(K^\perp\), conjugate by the inverse square root of the positive-definite compressed \(T(1)\), apply the normalized theorem, and conjugate back.
+
+Pointwise semidefinite Laplace positivity alone is insufficient. For example,
+\[
+\mathcal L_T(g)=
+\begin{pmatrix}1&g\\g&g^2\end{pmatrix}
+\succeq0
+\]
+is the transform of a distribution supported at zero, but its kernel varies with \(g\). In distribution notation,
+\[
+T=\begin{pmatrix}\delta&-\delta'\\-\delta'&\delta''\end{pmatrix},
+\qquad
+T*p=\begin{pmatrix}p&-p'\\-p'&p''\end{pmatrix}.
+\]
+A positive output would have \(p''\ge0\) and \(\int p''=0\), so \(p''=0\), incompatible with a positive integrable probability density.
+
+## 9. Polynomial and family consequences
+
+If a Hermitian matrix polynomial \(P(g)=\sum_\alpha P_\alpha g^\alpha\) satisfies \(P(g)\succ0\) for all real \(g\), then
+\[
+T=\sum_\alpha(-1)^{|\alpha|}P_\alpha\partial^\alpha\delta
+\]
+has real Laplace transform \(P(g)\). After normalizing \(P(0)\), the theorem gives a radial strictly log-concave \(p\in\mathscr E\) such that
+\[
+P(-\partial)p(x)\succ0\qquad\text{for every }x.
+\tag{36}
+\]
+This is an existence representation for positive polynomial symbols. It is not an algorithm for deciding polynomial positivity.
+
+The same \(q,L\) work for a family \(\{T_\omega\}\) if that family has common support, common finite-order seminorm bound, and
+\[
+\inf_{\omega,\,|g|\le t}
+d_C(\mathcal L_{T_\omega}(g))>0
+\quad\text{for every finite }t.
+\]
+The original bounded quantum tuples have the special transform \(e^{A(g)}\) and explicit exponential margins; their supplied candidate is recovered at the level of existence.
+
+No single fixed density works for every normalized Laplace-positive compact distribution without uniform seminorm/margin bounds. Already
+\(T_a=\delta+a\delta''\) has \(\mathcal L_{T_a}(g)=1+ag^2>0\) for all \(a>0\). A fixed smooth positive integrable \(p\) has \(p''<0\) somewhere—otherwise it would be convex and integrable—and \(p+ap''\) is negative there for sufficiently large \(a\).
+
+## 10. Provenance, novelty, and significance
+
+The attachment supplied the retain-the-tilt operation with an explicit exponential positivity margin. The equivalence, arbitrary-margin threshold construction, ordered-space form, singular-matrix classification, and deep-valley example above were reconstructed here. None of the attachment's Pauli obstruction, endpoint-gamma example, numerical checks, or practical claims are premises of this proof.
+
+Related work must be credited. Positive convolution multipliers have a long history. Katkova and Vishnyakova's 2001 Theorems 1–2 treat scalar one-dimensional functions with positive bilateral Laplace transform and positive endpoint neighborhoods; a Poisson-lattice convolution makes them nonnegative. Their multiplier is not radial or log-concave and their theorem has endpoint hypotheses. They cite Diamond and Essén (1978), whose precise scope still needs direct comparison. The finite lattice problem is related to Poincaré–Pólya–Handelman positivity multipliers and boundary faces. These precedents mean the general idea of repairing signs by positive convolution is not new.
+
+The candidate structural contribution is the exact criterion for arbitrary compact distributions with cone values, together with a scalar radial strictly log-concave regularizer carrying every exponential moment and no quantitative lower-margin hypothesis. Historical priority for that full statement is unresolved. The proof is internally complete subject to standard distribution and Paley–Wiener theorems, but has not received independent mathematical review.

+# Physical model challenge: layer-resolved electrochemical control
+
+**Disposition.** Tong et al.'s twisted-bilayer graphene (tBLG) experiment is a strong, independent counterexample to a one-knob transport model: at fixed total carrier density, the signed field and layer-resolved charge determine which layer reacts. It demonstrates an accessible, actively controlled operating regime and supports selective co-design. It does not falsify the supplied conditional passive-support theorem, establish that strain is irrelevant, or demonstrate a battery or civilization-scale advantage.
+
+## Model limitation and experimentally demonstrated operation
+
+A scalar description with one carrier density, one field magnitude, and one shared structural response cannot represent the following operation: hold total density fixed, reverse the perpendicular field, reverse proton flow, and select the other layer for hydrogenation while preserving a conductive layer. The minimal state must retain layer charges, layer reaction states, and signed field/proton direction. A useful bookkeeping state is
+
+\[
+x=(n_t,n_b,h_t,h_b,\operatorname{sgn}E,\text{proton-flow direction}),\qquad
+u=(V_t+V_b,V_t-V_b),\qquad n_{\rm tot}=n_t+n_b.
+\]
+
+The gate sum primarily sets total charge and the gate difference sets the perpendicular field; the paper's Methods also includes quantum-capacitance corrections. Under field-induced polarization, the individual layer densities can move differently at fixed total density. Equal total density and equal field magnitude therefore need not mean equal reaction state if the field sign is reversed.
+
+Tong et al. used a suspended tBLG device over a 10-µm aperture, with proton-conducting HTFSI/PEG electrolyte and PdHₓ gate electrodes. At fixed gate sum Vₜ+Vᵦ = 1 V, corresponding to n ≈ 5×10¹³ cm⁻²—below the ≈1×10¹⁴ cm⁻² monolayer hydrogenation threshold—the field drove proton transport and hydrogenated only the layer facing incoming protons. The other layer remained conductive. Reversing field polarity at fixed n reversed proton flow and selected the opposite layer. The single-layer insulating state persisted for more than 24 hours under fixed gates; lowering |E| below about 0.5 V nm⁻¹ at fixed n restored conductivity and removed the Raman D band. Selective cycling exceeded 1,000 cycles with electronic on/off ratio >10⁴ and cycle-to-cycle variation <6%.
+
+The measurements and the mechanism should be kept distinct. Figure 1 simultaneously records top- and bottom-layer in-plane conductance and out-of-plane proton current under opposite field polarities (the electronic source-drain biases are 2 mV). Raman D-band appearance supports hydrogenation. The layer-resolved carrier-density imbalance is the authors' electrostatic/analytical explanation, not a direct layer-charge measurement. The paper's E–n map and analytical model explain the transition boundaries by one layer reaching the hydrogenation threshold; these are not transferable coefficients for another interface.
+
+## Same-device simultaneous performance and strongest comparator
+
+The 2026 paper's Fig. 3 configures three logic modes in one tBLG device using the same square-wave gate inputs (−1.2 V and +2.4 V). The parallel electronic outputs implement layer-specific NOT gates, a tunnelling NOR, or a total-current NAND; the out-of-plane proton current supplies an XOR output in each mode. The main text gives an electronic on/off ratio of 10⁴ and a proton-current XOR ratio of 10². The Methods section instead says 10⁴ for the proton XOR, an internal discrepancy; use the conservative main-text value unless the figure or source data resolve it. This is a demonstrated same-device, same-input, configurable electronic/protonic operation—not a proposed Astra device.
+
+The strongest comparator is Tong et al.'s 2024 double-gated monolayer graphene experiment, which established independent control of field and density before the tBLG layer-selection result. With a single gate, proton transport drive and doping were coupled: around Vₜ ≈ 1.4 V, graphene conductivity fell by four orders of magnitude and a Raman D band appeared. With two gates, fixing the gate sum at 0.7 V while varying the difference drove strong proton current without hydrogenation; fixing the difference at zero while varying the sum suppressed proton flow but hydrogenated graphene. At n ≈ 10¹⁴ cm⁻², electron-doped graphene was about 30 times more proton-conductive than hole-doped graphene at the same density in the low-field regime, and at E > 0.5 V nm⁻¹ the current approached the electrolyte-limited current, with doping-dependent attenuation.
+
+The tBLG paper reports proton currents about 100 times lower than monolayer graphene at the same E. This is a cross-paper comparator, not a simultaneous matched-device head-to-head. The authors attribute the penalty to proton access being limited to AA regions (about 30% of area) and higher barriers: calculated 1.4 eV for the first layer and 1.7 eV for the second. The AB-stacked bilayer control is proton-impermeable and lacks layer-selective transitions. Thus tBLG buys layer selection and parallel logic, while losing substantially on proton flux; the evidence does not show that it improves net energy per useful proton or a practical membrane/battery metric.
+
+## A discriminating next measurement, not a claimed discovery
+
+The article demonstrates opposite layer selection under opposite field signs and separately demonstrates a low-field erase route. It does not establish whether reversing polarity directly swaps a prepared one-layer-hydrogenated state, first erases it, or transiently hydrogenates both. Test this by preparing each selected state at fixed n ≈ 5×10¹³ cm⁻², reversing signed E without an intervening erase step, and time-resolving both layer conductances, proton-current direction, Raman response, and gate charge. The outcomes distinguish direct layer-to-layer switching from sequential erase/re-hydrogenation or a doubly reacted transient. Acquire switching delay, transition probabilities, transferred charge, and flux under the same operating sequence before proposing quantitative control or transfer. The published opposite-polarity comparison already establishes layer selectivity; the proposed experiment only resolves the transition path.
+
+## Scope for co-design
+
+This evidence expands the intervention set beyond a fixed passive mechanical boundary: active electrostatic control plus an internal layer degree of freedom can separate transport from reaction and select where reaction occurs. That supports the possibility of useful/harmful process co-design, but it does not refute a conditional result about mechanical support under specified coefficients. Nor does it provide those coefficients or transfer the effect to hBN defects, Li-metal interfaces, or other battery geometries. A separate 2026 double-gated Li⁺ study reports independent density/rate control in a micron-scale interfacial channel, but it is not a through-plane hBN/Cu battery test and is not needed to establish the graphene result.
+
+## Primary sources
+
+- J. Tong et al., [“Layer-selective hydrogenation and proton transport in twisted bilayer graphene,” Nature Communications 17, 4873 (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-71147-y). See Figs. 1–3 and Methods; source data are linked at [Zenodo record 18783917](https://zenodo.org/records/18783917), not downloaded for this note.

+# Transient isotope separation: a real operation, but no new qualified capability
+
+Status: **NOT_ACHIEVED**. Independent physical-operation investigation, 15 October 2026. No laboratory experiment, new material simulation, purchase, or outside communication was performed. Both supplied pasted-text attachments were read completely. Their missing packages were not used as premises or treated as a research task. No sibling research output was consulted during selection.
+
+The selected operation was a sequence of **load, close, selectively purge, and harvest** in one hydrogen-isotope adsorbent. It attacks molecular separation rather than passive mechanical de-trapping. Stable-isotope supply supports scientific experiments, chemical analysis, and semiconductor processing. It would not itself establish energy abundance: useful deuterium separation and an economical fusion energy system are different capabilities.
+
+The selection had an experimental reason. Real frameworks already combine temperature-dependent access, isotope discrimination, storage, and release. This avoids inventing a favorable response matrix. The investigation nevertheless found two decisive limits: the broad sequence is established prior art, and the proposed extra purification pulse lacks the mixed-feed escape contrast needed for useful recovery. A short room-temperature graphene alternative also failed qualification.
+
+## One obtainable apparatus and the proposed operation
+
+The concrete substrate is a packed **Cu-ZIF-gis** bed with temperature control, inlet isolation, pressure control, and separately collected outlet fractions. The candidate sequence was:
+
+1. Admit a declared H2/D2 mixture while pores are accessible.
+2. Cool and isolate the bed to trap the loaded molecules.
+3. Open a selected release window and discard an H-rich fraction.
+4. Release the retained D-rich fraction into a product receiver and restore the initial state.
+
+The apparatus does not require an arbitrary atom clamp, an assumed hidden actuator, or a material assembled from different papers. But the useful properties must hold **for this sequence and this feed**. Storage and release alone do not establish selective purification.
+
+The primary Cu-ZIF-gis paper reports 1:1 H2/D2 loading for 60 minutes, evacuation, cooling to 18 K, and a 6 K/min release ramp to 240 K. At 120 K and 2 bar its TDS selectivity is approximately 1.7; Fig. 3d gives roughly 0.45 mmol D2/g by visual reading. Separate breakthrough measurements used 1.832 g of pellets and Ne/H2/D2 = 95.11/2.45/2.45 vol%, 3.68 cc/min: dynamic selectivities were 1.5 at 115 K and 1.3 at 159 K. Room-temperature dosing followed by cold trapping and thermal release was already demonstrated. These are published measurements, not Astra results. [Jung et al., 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-56649-5)
+
+**Novelty decision:** warm loading, temporary gate closure, and later release cannot be claimed as a new invention. The only remaining proposal was whether a separately harvested purification window improves the complete recovery/energy frontier. The available measurements do not establish this. No additional hypothetical waveform should be optimized without measuring that gate.
+
+## The coupled requirement that an extra purge must satisfy
+
+Let `n_H(0)` and `n_D(0)` be the amounts retained immediately before a purge. Count molecules of the same declared species; this two-species treatment excludes chemical conversion and isotope exchange. During a one-way, feed-free purge with no re-adsorption, define cumulative effective escape exposures
+
+\[
+\Lambda_i=-\log[n_i(t)/n_i(0)],\qquad i\in\{H,D\}.
+\]
+
+The odds gain and desired-isotope retention are then exactly
+
+\[
+A=\frac{n_D(t)/n_H(t)}{n_D(0)/n_H(0)}
+ =e^{\Lambda_H-\Lambda_D},
+\qquad R_D=e^{-\Lambda_D}.
+\]
+
+For a target gain `A > 1`, positive desired-isotope loss, and retention at least `0 < R < 1`, a necessary condition is
+
+\[
+\boxed{\frac{\Lambda_H}{\Lambda_D}
+\ge 1+\frac{\log A}{-\log R}.}
+\]
+
+This is a screening identity, not a new fundamental theorem or a fitted material model. If every allowed interval has an effective unwanted/desired escape ratio at most `r_max`, splitting the purge into multiple windows cannot evade
+
+\[
+A\le R_D^{-(r_{\max}-1)}.
+\]
+
+Zero desired-isotope loss with positive unwanted-isotope escape is the ideal infinite-ratio limit; no finite ratio is assigned to it.
+
+| Retain captured D | Escape-exposure ratio required to double odds | Required for tenfold odds |
+|---|---:|---:|
+| 99% | 69.97 | 230.11 |
+| 95% | 14.51 | 45.89 |
+| 90% | 7.58 | 22.85 |
+| 80% | 4.11 | 11.32 |
+
+For the 1.7-odds starting example, doubling odds yields only `3.4/(1+3.4) = 77.3%` D2 in the retained two-species fraction. Ninety-percent retention here concerns **already captured D2**, not 90% recovery from the inlet. Total feed recovery additionally includes loading, dead-volume removal, harvesting, and any recycle losses.
+
+In a reversible dilute-site kinetic model, detailed balance additionally couples entry and escape:
+
+\[
+K_i=k_{\mathrm{in},i}/k_{\mathrm{out},i},
+\qquad
+\frac{k_{\mathrm{out},H}}{k_{\mathrm{out},D}}
+=\frac{K_D/K_H}{k_{\mathrm{in},D}/k_{\mathrm{in},H}}.
+\]
+
+Thus faster desired-species entry and stronger desired-species binding are not independent multiplicative gifts. This simple model is **not** assigned to the hysteretic Cu framework, and no source-derived rate is inferred from it. It explains why the actual mixed-feed release trace is indispensable. Localized single-gas mobility, an equilibrium affinity, or an entry selectivity does not supply the required escape exposures.

+If HD forms or molecules re-adsorb, the simple purge calculation is inapplicable. The experiment must then track atomic isotope balances and the actual product fractions directly. Adding an unobserved exchange reaction to restore a favorable answer is not permitted.

+
+A recent theory also explicitly studies mass-selective transport through fluctuating nanopores, including proposed external modulation. It is not a laboratory demonstration of a new pulsed separator. It removes a broad priority claim for deliberately exploiting a molecular gate's timescale. [Tang et al., 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-026-75540-5)
+
+## Full-cycle cost and scale
+
+Use a common contract: the same declared H2/HD/D2 composition, feed pressure and temperature, impurities, final purity, isotope recovery, output pressure, and delivered amount. For the first comparison, a prepared 1:1 H2/D2 gas feed is legitimate **only if every method receives that feed and its preparation cost is stated separately**. A natural-water capability requires a different experiment.

+For an atomic D fraction `x` after randomized molecular pairing,

+\[

+\]

+## Short qualification of a different room-temperature state sequence
+
+A second candidate was an electrochemical **isotope capture-and-release electrode**: selectively deuterate graphene, remove weakly retained H, then release retained D into another reservoir. The relevant paper demonstrates reversible hydrogenation and deuteration, an isotope-dependent potential shift, and roughly `10^14` adsorbed hydrons/cm2. Its device has a 15 µm exposed hole; hydrogen evolution competes with storage. Crucially, its isotope substitution tests use separate proton/deuteron electrolytes, not a mixed-feed separator. [Soong et al., 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-025-65771-3)
+
+Capacity arithmetic is decisive for what may presently be claimed. At that density, the exposed microdevice holds only `2.93\times10^-16` mol of hydrons, or 0.59 femtogram if every site carries D. Even one square metre of active surface stores at most 1.66 micromol, or 3.34 micrograms of D, at the stated density. These upper-bound calculations grant neither all-D occupation in a mixture nor collection into a product stream.
+
+Electrical switching can be technologically valuable for memory, but that is already the source's application. It supplies no measured mixture purity, reservoir exchange, or bulk isotope turnover. Higher surface area and faster hypothetical fluid switching would introduce a new unqualified apparatus. **Stop this separation proposal at qualification.**
+
+## Disposition
+
+Retain the explicit purity–retention screening identity and the source-linked capacity calculations as negative research results. The isotope-sequence investigation found a physically real and interesting operation, already developed by others, and identified what additional purge would have to demonstrate. It did not discover a new qualified physical capability or establish a lower-cost isotope technology. No further conditional cycle modeling is warranted without the actual mixed-feed release measurement.
+
+The supplied hBN and adjoint attachments informed the requirement that effects and access coexist in one apparatus. No favorable coefficient, missing artifact, or claimed earlier success was imported into this route.

+"""Source-linked arithmetic and analytic thresholds; no simulated material data.
+
+Run from any directory with Python 3. Writes screening_calculations.json beside
+this file. The approximate Cu-ZIF-gis capacity is a visual Fig. 3d reading, not
+raw source data. All-D graphene occupation is an upper-bound scenario.
+"""
+
+import json
+import math
+from pathlib import Path
+
+AVOGADRO = 6.02214076e23
+DEUTERIUM_ATOM_G_PER_MOL = 2.01410177812
+
+
+def compute():
+    thresholds = []
+    for retained in (0.99, 0.95, 0.9, 0.8, 0.5):
+        for gain in (2.0, 10.0):
+            thresholds.append({
+                "retained_D_fraction": retained,
+                "additional_odds_gain": gain,
+                "required_H_to_D_integrated_escape_ratio":
+                    1 + math.log(gain) / -math.log(retained),
+            })
+
+    density_cm2 = 1e14
+    area_micro_cm2 = math.pi * (15e-4 / 2) ** 2
+    stored_micro_mol = density_cm2 * area_micro_cm2 / AVOGADRO
+    stored_mol_per_m2 = density_cm2 * 1e4 / AVOGADRO
+    return {
+        "status": "NOT_ACHIEVED",
+        "calculation_type": "analytic screening thresholds and source-linked arithmetic; no material simulation",
+        "purge_thresholds": thresholds,
+        "graphene_capacity": {
+            "source_adsorbed_atoms_per_cm2": density_cm2,
+            "source_exposed_hole_diameter_um": 15.0,
+            "microdevice_area_cm2": area_micro_cm2,
+            "microdevice_max_stored_hydrons_mol": stored_micro_mol,
+            "microdevice_mass_if_all_D_femtograms":
+                stored_micro_mol * DEUTERIUM_ATOM_G_PER_MOL * 1e15,
+            "max_stored_hydrons_mol_per_m2": stored_mol_per_m2,
+            "mass_if_all_D_micrograms_per_m2":
+                stored_mol_per_m2 * DEUTERIUM_ATOM_G_PER_MOL * 1e6,
+            "scope": "Capacity arithmetic only. All-D occupation is an upper-bound scenario, not measured mixture separation.",
+        },
+        "CuZIF_gis_protocol_arithmetic": {
+            "mixed_D2_uptake_mmol_per_g_figure_read": 0.45,
+            "figure_read_precision": "Approximate visual Fig. 3d reading; 120 K, 2 bar, 1:1 H2:D2, published TDS protocol",
+            "exposure_min": 60.0,
+            "readout_ramp_start_K": 18.0,
+            "readout_ramp_end_K": 240.0,
+            "ramp_K_per_min": 6.0,
+            "readout_ramp_min": (240 - 18) / 6,
+            "exposure_plus_ramp_min": 60 + (240 - 18) / 6,
+            "capacity_divided_by_exposure_plus_ramp_mmol_per_g_per_h":
+                0.45 / ((60 + (240 - 18) / 6) / 60),
+            "scope": "Protocol arithmetic excludes cooling, evacuation and losses; not measured production throughput or a universal bound.",
+        },
+        "random_pairing_at_illustrative_atomic_D_fraction": {
+            "x": 1.5e-4,
+            "H2": (1 - 1.5e-4) ** 2,
+            "HD": 2 * 1.5e-4 * (1 - 1.5e-4),
+            "D2": (1.5e-4) ** 2,
+            "scope": "Combinatorial scenario; does not establish that a particular feed is equilibrated.",
+        },
+        "Carnot_refrigeration_at_ambient_298K": [
+            {"cold_temperature_K": t,
+             "minimum_refrigerator_work_J_per_J_heat_at_constant_T": 298 / t - 1}
+            for t in (18.0, 23.3, 60.0, 77.0, 115.0, 120.0, 159.0)
+        ],
+        "doubled_1p7_odds_D_fraction": 3.4 / 4.4,
+    }
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":

+Scalar acquisition of a reusable nonreciprocal control-response map
+Independent discovery packet, 2026-10-15
+
+Disposition: conditional exact mathematical construction and synthetic checks.
+Physical capability advantage, research priority, and mission achievement are
+NOT ESTABLISHED. This operation was selected independently of the port-adjoint
+framework. It changes the operator through actual controls and learns a reusable
+scalar response map. It does not reconstruct an adjoint field.
+
+1. Scientific opportunity and exact interface
+
+The scientific task is to predict a fixed externally observed response under
+many future combinations of local controls, through an otherwise unknown linear
+network. This is relevant to programmable scattering, circuit response shaping,
+and linearized transport. No benefit for an unknown nonlinear plant is claimed.
+
+Assume the apparatus supplies, at a fixed frequency or in steady state,
+
+    A(u) = A + P diag(u) P^T,
+    f(u) = c^T A(u)^(-1) b,
+
+where A is invertible, u has m components, and all queried operators are
+invertible. The columns of P specify independently calibrated additive rank-one
+actuator changes. b is the ordinary source and c specifies a detector. Physical
+injection of c, internal field readout, reciprocity, known nonreciprocal support,
+and physical reversal are unnecessary. Source and detector may coincide.
+
+Indispensable supplied or separately acquired facts are linearity over the
+operating range, fixed A,b,c during calibration and reuse, the additive rank-one
+actuator laws and their independence, actual values of each applied u, stable
+settling, and repeatable return to the reference configuration. The theorem
+does not acquire or certify those premises from scalar responses.
+
+Let
+
+    H = P^T A^(-1) P,
+    w = P^T A^(-1) b,
+    v^T = c^T A^(-1) P,
+    f0 = c^T A^(-1) b.
+
+Woodbury gives, with D=diag(u),
+
+    f(u) = f0 - v^T D (I + H D)^(-1) w.                 (1)
+
+The formula also holds if some u_i vanish. For generic w_i != 0, put W=diag(w)
+and use the diagonal gauge Hbar=W^(-1) H W and a_i=v_i w_i. Since W commutes
+with every allowed D,
+
+    f(u) = f0 - a^T D (I + Hbar D)^(-1) 1.              (2)
+
+The estimator learns f0,a,Hbar from scalar queries. It does not learn the
+original full A. Below, H denotes Hbar for economy.
+
+2. Generic exact theorem
+
+Fix two distinct positive values t1,t2 and another positive value t3. They must
+be physically permissible and all proposed inverses must exist. For generic
+real coefficients (f0,a,H), the following schedule reconstructs the complete
+function (2), for every future u at which its inverse exists, using exactly
+
+    Q(m) = (3 m^2 - m + 4)/2
+
+scalar queries for m>=2. For m=1 it uses three queries. "Generic" means outside
+a finite union of explicitly described algebraic exceptional sets. This is
+not a uniform conditioning or noisy-data theorem.
+
+The schedule is one baseline, two singleton settings per control, two settings
+per pair of controls, m-2 anchored triple settings, and one triple setting for
+each pair among controls 3,...,m. No configuration activates more than three
+controls. The control hardware needs the reference and two distinct nonzero
+values; a strictly binary actuator does not provide this schedule.
+
+2.1 Singleton acquisitions
+
+For one active control i at value t, let delta_i(t)=f0-f(t e_i). Then
+
+    delta_i(t) = a_i t/(1+d_i t),  d_i=H_ii.
+
+Two values identify d_i and a_i:
+
+    d_i = [delta_i(t2)/t2 - delta_i(t1)/t1]
+          /[delta_i(t1)-delta_i(t2)],
+    a_i = delta_i(t1)(1+d_i t1)/t1.
+
+We exclude a_i=0 and the vanishing denominators. These exclusions are essential.
+
+2.2 Pair acquisitions
+
+For active controls i,j with values s,t define x=H_ij, y=H_ji,
+p=xy, q=a_i x+a_j y, and delta=f0-f(s e_i+t e_j). Direct inversion gives
+
+    delta = [a_i s + a_j t
+              +(a_i d_j+a_j d_i-q)st]
+            /[1+d_i s+d_j t+(d_i d_j-p)st].             (3)
+
+For each measured delta, all quantities in
+
+    q - delta p = r,
+    r = [a_i s+a_j t+(a_i d_j+a_j d_i)st
+         -delta(1+d_i s)(1+d_j t)]/(st)
+
+are now known except p,q. Two settings, in the implementation (s,t)=(t1,t1)
+and (t2,t2), identify p,q provided their deltas differ. The two possible directed
+entries are given by the roots of
+
+    a_i x^2 - q x + a_j p = 0,
+    y = (q-a_i x)/a_j.
+
+The two possibilities are
+
+    (x,y) and ((a_j/a_i)y, (a_i/a_j)x).                 (4)
+
+The quadratic discriminant is exactly (a_i x-a_j y)^2. Near weighted
+reciprocity, root selection is ill conditioned. Complex roots from noisy real
+data are a model-consistency warning, not a valid new physical response.
+
+2.3 Aligning pair choices with triples
+
+Choose either solution for edge {1,2}. For each k>=3, retain that edge and
+enumerate the four combinations of pair choices for {1,k} and {2,k}. Compare
+the four predicted responses to one actual measurement with u_1=u_2=u_k=t3.
+Under the generic separation condition, precisely one choice matches.
+
+This establishes all edges incident to controls 1 or 2. For each 3<=i<j<=m,
+enumerate the two choices for {i,j}, with {1,i},{1,j} already fixed. One actual
+measurement with u_1=u_i=u_j=t3 selects the matching choice, again assuming
+nonzero candidate separation.
+
+To justify generic separation, all candidate responses are rational functions
+of a,d and off-diagonal entries. Equality of two distinct candidates, after
+clearing nonsingular denominators, is an algebraic condition. None of these
+equalities is an identically zero polynomial: one witness, also checked with
+exact rational arithmetic in the script, is
+
+    a=(1,2,3), f0=10,
+       [10   1/5    1/2 ]
+    H= [3/10 10    11/10],   t3=1.
+       [7/10 13/10 10   ]
+
+Holding edge {1,2} fixed and independently switching the two other edge choices
+produces the four distinct scalar responses
+
+    12487600/1311109,
+    37462120/3933429,
+    37473360/3934847,
+    12489080/1311287.
+
+This witnesses every four-choice separation condition after relabelling. It
+also witnesses the two-choice conditions. The other inversion denominators
+and pair-root separations are nonzero on generic coefficients. A finite union
+of proper algebraic exceptional sets has empty interior. Strictly dissipative
+plants form an open family, so these generic conditions do not exclude all
+physically dissipative plants.
+
+2.4 What ambiguity survives, and why it does not change the allowed decisions
+
+Let R=diag(a) and define
+
+    Hstar = R^(-1) H^T R.
+
+Transposing the scalar expression and using
+(I+D H)^(-1)D=D(I+H D)^(-1) proves
+
+    a^T D(I+Hstar D)^(-1)1 = a^T D(I+H D)^(-1)1.        (5)
+
+If the initial edge {1,2} was chosen in the original orientation, uniqueness
+of every subsequent triple selection reconstructs H. If it was chosen in the
+other orientation, the same argument reconstructs Hstar. Both are compatible
+with all acquired data, and (5) proves identical predictions under every
+permitted diagonal control. Physical orientation of hidden edges is therefore
+unnecessary for this fixed scalar prediction task. Coupled controls, a changed
+source, or a changed detector can make the ambiguity relevant and are outside
+this theorem.
+
+The query count is
+
+    1 + 2m + 2 C(m,2) + (m-2) + C(m-2,2)
+      = (3m^2-m+4)/2.
+
+The reconstruction performs O(m^2) constant-sized algebraic operations and
+stores O(m^2) numbers. A dense prediction uses an m-dimensional linear solve,
+ordinarily O(m^3) arithmetic. This does not solve global discrete optimization
+over m controls in polynomial time.
+
+3. Exact failure of uniform robustness for the fixed-anchor schedule
+
+Let the two anchor nodes be disconnected, in H, from an interior three-node
+block. Use the above H for that interior block in one system. In the other,
+switch only its edge {1,3} according to (4). Keep a=(1,2,1,2,3) for the
+five-control plant. Every queried configuration in the fixed-anchor schedule
+contains at most two interior controls. By (3), every acquired scalar response
+is therefore identical in the two systems. The unqueried interior triple gives
+responses differing by exactly
+
+    5135840960/5159013315323 = approximately 0.0009955083746.
+
+Arbitrarily small generic perturbations of anchor-interior links can leave the
+exceptional set while leaving that future difference fixed. Because this is
+an open dense algebraic condition, such perturbations exist arbitrarily near
+the disconnected example. The illustrative executed epsilon=1e-6 perturbation
+differs on all calibration queries by at most 4.02e-9; that particular floating
+point instance was not separately certified against every generic-condition
+polynomial. Thus there is no uniform
+noise-robustness bound for this fixed schedule on all generic plants. Choosing
+better anchors or adding diverse joint configurations can fix this particular
+example, but their cost and guarantees require separate analysis.
+
+4. Stronger obstruction: all proper-subset experiments can be insufficient
+
+For any even m>=4, let d=1+1/m, f0=2m, and let C_sigma be a directed cyclic
+permutation matrix whose cycle product is sigma=+1 or -1. Exactly one edge
+changes sign between the two cases. Define
+
+    H_sigma=d I + C_sigma,
+    w=v=e_1,
+              [2m    e_1^T]
+    G_sigma = [e_1   H_sigma],
+    A_sigma=G_sigma^(-1).
+
+Here G is the complete response matrix, including the external source/detector
+coordinate. Both systems are strictly dissipative. Indeed sym(H_sigma)>=I/m.
+The Schur complement of sym(H_sigma) in sym(G_sigma) is at least
+2m-m=m>0. More quantitatively, Young's inequality yields
+sym(G_sigma)>=I/(3m), and ||G_sigma||<=2m+3. Hence
+
+    cond(A_sigma)=cond(G_sigma)<=3m(2m+3),
+
+so no exponential matrix conditioning is required. Inverting preserves strict
+positivity of the symmetric part: sym(A)=G^(-T) sym(G) G^(-1)>0. Adding any
+nonnegative diagonal conductance keeps the physical admittance strictly
+dissipative.
+
+Let r_i=u_i/(1+d u_i). The directly observed one-port response is exactly
+
+    f_sigma(u)=2m-r_1/[1+(-1)^(m-1) sigma product_i(r_i)]. (6)
+
+If any u_i=0, then product_i(r_i)=0. Consequently the two systems agree under
+EVERY configuration that changes fewer than all m controls, at arbitrary
+nonnegative amplitudes. This is an exact statement, not a finite random test.
+
+For u_i=m for all i, put r=m/(m+2). The response difference is
+
+    2 r^(m+1)/(1-r^(2m)) -> 1/sinh(2) > 0.
+
+It remains of constant size as m grows. At m=32 the difference is 0.276209.
+More strongly, the two candidate actions u=m*1 and u=2m*1 are ranked oppositely
+for minimizing the scalar response: at m=32 their response differences are
+-0.142825 in the sigma=+1 plant and +0.046862 in the sigma=-1 plant.
+
+This demonstrates genuine missing action information under low-order
+calibration, even for a known additive rank-one actuator family and dissipative
+operators. It does NOT prove exponentially many experiments are necessary:
+one suitable full-support measurement distinguishes this pair. It does show
+why a universal claim cannot follow from only singleton, pair, or triple
+validation. The collective controls here have amplitudes O(m), total applied
+conductance O(m^2), and nonzero switching/reset costs. These are charged inputs.
+
+5. What was executed
+
+check_scalar_acquisition.py used only its scalar oracle in the estimator.
+Eight seeded dense strictly dissipative nonreciprocal plants were tested for
+each m in {3,8,16,32} and each absolute additive response-noise standard
+deviation in {0,1e-10,1e-8,1e-6,1e-4}. There are 100 independent held-out
+control configurations per run. Failed real-root estimates were counted.
+
+Noiseless median held-out response RMS errors were 3.90e-15, 4.12e-14,
+4.12e-13, and 1.78e-12, respectively. At m=32, Q=1522. Absolute response noise
+1e-4 yielded median response RMS error 0.547 and error 0.798 relative to the
+control-induced response. At noise 1e-6 those figures were 0.00533 and 0.00802;
+however 1137 pair estimates across the eight runs had nonreal candidate roots,
+so these complex intermediate models are not qualified physical models.
+
+The separate high-order script checked (6) against direct loaded-plant inverses
+for m=4,6,10,16,32,64. Every sampled proper-subset difference was zero; the
+largest direct-inverse/formula discrepancy was 8.53e-14. The all-subset equality
+itself follows from (6), not from those sampled checks.
+
+These are synthetic normalized examples. They contain no measured seconds,
+joules, fabrication response, ADC tolerance, calibration lifetime or physical
+demonstration. They establish neither a new hardware capability nor superior
+performance over the strongest model-fitting comparator.
+
+A separate executed three-level schedule, t1=1,t2=2,t3=1, is saved in
+ternary_acquisition_results.json and check_ternary_acquisition.py. At m=32,
+eight noiseless seeds again used 1522 queries, with median held-out RMS error
+3.27e-12 and maximum 6.29e-11. Absolute response noise 1e-4 produced median RMS
+error 0.684 and error 0.999 relative to the control-induced response. These
+results show that the exact construction is executable on ternary controls;
+they do not remove its noise failure. The earlier four-level results remain
+preserved separately. A complete 94-query ternary m=8 synthetic measurement
+receipt and both true/acquired normalized models are saved in
+ternary_example_receipt.json. No binary-only acquisition theorem was proved.
+
+6. Full-cost comparison and disposition
+
+See COSTS_AND_COMPARATORS.txt for primary literature, matched interfaces and
+cost accounting. The strongest prior physical route already learns a reusable
+response model from external measurements. This construction is a possible
+closed-form generic initialization or calibration schedule for that route.
+Its mathematical contribution is potentially useful, but priority is not
+established and the operation does not yet meet the civilization-scale mission.
+
+The decisive next experiment, if this instrument niche is pursued, is a blind
+scalar-response calibration of an actual many-control nonreciprocal apparatus,
+with known load values and held-out collective configurations, compared at
+equal source time, scalar reads, switching, precision and calibration reuse to
+physics-compliant model fitting. A simulation cannot substitute for that gate.

+2026-10-15
+
+Result: an explicit generic exact acquisition schedule, plus decisive failures
+of universal low-order qualification and of uniform robustness. No laboratory
+demonstration, novelty finding, total-cost win, or mission achievement.

+1. Strong primary comparators, read in this investigation
+
+A. Sol, Prod'homme, Le Magoarou and del Hougne, Nature Communications 15, 2841
+(2024), "Experimentally realized physical-model-based frugal wave control in
+metasurface-programmable complex media."
+https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-024-46916-2
+
+This is the strongest directly relevant physical baseline: acquiring a compact
+reusable wave-response model from externally measured random configurations.
+Their study includes prediction of one complex transmission coefficient and
+larger accessible scattering matrices, then experimental wave control. The
+reported 68-control cavity is reciprocal; it is not evidence for this new
+nonreciprocal closed-form schedule. Their SISO calibration and task-focused
+ambiguity tolerance already preempt a broad claim that scalar external data
+can newly enable reusable control prediction. An equally informed comparator
+must fit the same nonreciprocal rational model family to the same scalar data,
+with multiple starts, noise treatment, calibration and independent joint
+configurations. This comparator was not numerically executed here.
+
+B. Del Hougne, "Virtual VNA 3.0: Unambiguous Scattering Matrix Estimation for
+Non-Reciprocal Systems by Leveraging Tunable and Coupled Loads" (2025).
+https://arxiv.org/html/2503.07239v1
+
+This experimentally characterizes nonreciprocal networks using multiple
+accessible VNA ports, three known individual terminations at each hidden port,
+and known coupled loads. Its objective is an unambiguous full scattering
+matrix. The quoted closed-form configuration count is 1+3m+m(m-1)/2 for more
+than two accessible ports, with an extra setting in the two-port case.
+Each setting returns a matrix, not one scalar. The present construction
+predicts only a fixed scalar channel under future independent loads and
+therefore permits diagonal-gauge and weighted-transpose ambiguity. It supplies
+less information and uses a different physical interface. It has not beaten
+Virtual VNA experimentally. The paper also explicitly distinguishes useful
+channel prediction from unnecessary removal of internal ambiguity.
+
+C. Aravind, Chatterjee, Ghosh, Gurjar, Raj and Saha, "Learning Read-Once
+Determinants and the Principal Minor Assignment Problem" (2026; STOC 2026).
+https://arxiv.org/html/2603.04255v1
+https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3798129.3800875
+
+This provides randomized polynomial-time exact algebraic reconstruction of
+read-once determinants and black-box principal-minor assignment. It is a
+stronger general algebraic comparator than an exponential table of control
+settings. Its field-operation model is not a noisy physical-measurement model.
+A scalar transfer-response oracle is not automatically a determinant oracle;
+converting between them can introduce pole-cancellation and precision gates.
+The current quadratic schedule is derived directly from scalar responses and
+does not implement or claim to improve their general learner.
+
+The primary-literature search did not establish priority for this particular
+generic anchored-triple construction. The underlying Woodbury response model,
+load-modulation acquisition, and task-preserving ambiguity are established
+ideas. No "first" or new physical-capability claim is justified.
+
+2. Matched information and exact configuration counts
+
+One acquisition configuration means: set the actual operator through calibrated
+actuators, allow settling, apply the fixed ordinary source, and read the fixed
+detector. Source profile can remain unchanged while the operator changes.
+Each configuration still incurs operating-point acquisition and settling.
+
+At m=32, the present exact schedule uses:
+
+    baseline                         1
+    singleton configurations        64
+    pair configurations             992
+    anchor triples                  30
+    other anchored triples          435
+    total                           1522
+
+Each read is one signed real scalar for a real steady circuit. A complex
+coherent wave coefficient contains two real quadratures and needs a phase
+reference. Intensity-only measurements do not supply the signed/complex values
+used in this proof. Bit precision, repetitions, integration time and ADC noise
+must be charged independently of the configuration count.
+
+The hardware needs three calibrated values per actuator: reference, t1, t2.
+The triple value t3 may equal one of the nonzero values, although the script
+uses a third nonzero value for convenience. The proof's exhibited algebraic
+separation witness uses t3=1; a three-state hardware schedule can instead choose
+t1=1,t2=2,t3=1, and the same generic-separation argument applies. The script's
+initial tested values are reference 0, t1=.5,t2=1.5,t3=1 (four physical levels).
+The separate check_ternary_acquisition.py subsequently executed t1=1,t2=2,t3=1
+on eight m=32 seeds per noise level. Its 1522 scalar configurations use exactly
+three physical levels {0,1,2}. Both result sets are preserved. These are scalar
+configuration counts, not binary-tuner counts. A binary-only apparatus cannot
+execute the present singleton identification. No binary-tuner query bound was
+proved.
+
+If every query is reset independently to reference, the upper count of scalar
+actuator writes (set and reset both counted) is
+
+    4m + 8 C(m,2) + 6[(m-2)+C(m-2,2)]
+      = 7m^2-9m+6,
+
+or 6886 writes at m=32. Better ordering can reduce writes. Reset hysteresis,
+thermal memory and actuator latency were not measured. Neither the physical
+source energy nor controller/ADC energy was measured.
+
+3. Full cost ledger and reuse limits
+
+Acquisition hardware: one stable source and one fixed detector (possibly at
+the same port); m independently switchable calibrated rank-one controls;
+known reference impedances or conductance increments. Fabrication and access
+to m controllable terminations are supplied inputs, not gained by algebra.
+
+Calibration: actual actuator values and independence, source gain/phase and
+loading, detector gain/phase, stationary reference planes, linearity and
+repeatability. Unknown actuator cross-coupling can invalidate A+PDP^T. Multiple
+calibration settings can test the premise but finite tests do not certify an
+arbitrary unknown nonlinear actuator law.
+
+Time: at least Q distinct settled operating points for the exact schedule,
+multiplied by repetitions and integration required by precision. A nominal
+single measurement is not a fixed number of seconds. Calibration lifetime
+must exceed the complete acquisition and reuse block.
+
+Precision: the singleton inverse uses differences of scalar responses; pair
+reconstruction divides by another response difference; quadratic roots and
+triangle selection require further separation. An exact nonzero margin may
+be far below available noise. For independent Gaussian measurement noise of
+standard deviation sigma0, distinguishing a known candidate separation gamma
+by repeated averaging ordinarily requires at least order sigma0^2/gamma^2
+samples. This is not a sufficient end-to-end bound because estimated pair
+candidates also carry uncertainty. Weak-anchor separations approach zero,
+so no uniform finite precision follows from genericity.
+
+Control/reset: every experiment changes real controls; objective disturbance,
+switching wear, settling and reset are costs. The high-order counterexample
+needs collective amplitudes O(m) and total conductance O(m^2) for its constant
+future response gap; those are declared resources, not a free amplification.
+
+Computation/storage: O(m^2) scalar coefficients and reconstruction work in the
+ideal field model; ordinarily O(m^3) arithmetic for each dense future response.
+Many binary configurations still create a combinatorial optimization problem.
+No polynomial global optimizer was supplied.
+
+Reuse: all predictions concern the same A,b,c and the same additive calibrated
+control family. Drift, altered source illumination, a new objective detector,
+frequency change, nonlinear operating-point change or beyond-diagonal controls
+can require new calibration. A response-model ambiguity that is harmless for
+the original task need not be harmless for the changed task.
+
+4. What would count as an advantage
+
+For q requested future scalar predictions, a direct measurement baseline uses
+q actual configurations and naturally includes the same actuator/readout
+noise. An acquired model pays Q repetitions plus calibration, then digital
+prediction costs. Its nominal amortization only begins when q is sufficiently
+larger than Q and the plant stays fixed. This is the same reuse benefit already
+provided by measured-model methods; it is not newly established here.
+
+The relevant other baseline is physics-compliant rational model fitting using
+the same observable scalar, same known actuator values, same allowed joint
+configurations and same acquisition budget. It can fit all data jointly and
+regularize small interactions, avoiding brittle hard branch choices. Its
+optimization may be nonconvex; a favorable initialization is a possible use
+of the present exact construction. No matched comparison has shown that this
+improvement dominates total experimental cost.
+
+For one or a few immediate control decisions, direct finite interventions or
+stochastic optimization can be cheaper than acquiring an entire reusable map.
+Coordinate finite differences with two measurements per parameter are not the
+only legitimate baseline. The candidate has no demonstrated advantage over
+well-tuned stochastic control on a matched physical task.
+
+5. Stop decision
+
+The broad scientific operation already has strong physical prior art. The
+explicit generic exact schedule may be useful mathematical capital, but its
+fixed-anchor robustness is decisively limited and its additional measurement
+levels are real hardware requirements. The proper-subset counterexample
+shows that weak assumptions about collective controls cannot be repaired by
+more singleton/pair validation. This route should be preserved as secondary
+exact acquisition and negative robustness work, without further capability
+promotion until a measured, matched apparatus test changes the evidence.

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Dissipative plants invisible to every proper-subset control experiment."""
+import json
+from pathlib import Path
+import numpy as np
+
+
+def build(m, sign):
+    d=1+1/m
+    H=d*np.eye(m)
+    for i in range(m):
+        H[i,(i+1)%m]=1
+    H[0,1]=sign
+    w=np.eye(m)[0]
+    G=np.block([[np.array([[2*m]]),w[None,:]],[w[:,None],H]])
+    return G,H
+
+
+def formula(m, sign, u):
+    d=1+1/m
+    ratios=u/(1+d*u)
+    return 2*m-ratios[0]/(1+(-1)**(m-1)*sign*np.prod(ratios))
+
+
+results=[]
+for m in (4,6,10,16,32,64):
+    Gp,Hp=build(m,1)
+    Gn,Hn=build(m,-1)
+    Ap,An=np.linalg.inv(Gp),np.linalg.inv(Gn)
+    rng=np.random.default_rng(900+m)
+    errors=[]; sparse_differences=[]
+    for _ in range(100):
+        u=rng.uniform(0,2*m,m)
+        u[rng.integers(m)]=0
+        fp=formula(m,1,u); fn=formula(m,-1,u)
+        sparse_differences.append(abs(fp-fn))
+        for A,sign in ((Ap,1),(An,-1)):
+            D=np.diag(np.r_[0.,u]); b=np.eye(m+1)[0]
+            errors.append(abs(np.linalg.solve(A+D,b)[0]-formula(m,sign,u)))
+    u=np.full(m,float(m)); v=np.full(m,float(2*m))
+    pf,pv=formula(m,1,u),formula(m,1,v)
+    nf,nv=formula(m,-1,u),formula(m,-1,v)
+    results.append({"m":m,
+       "min_symmetric_G_plus_eigenvalue":float(np.linalg.eigvalsh((Gp+Gp.T)/2).min()),
+       "min_symmetric_G_minus_eigenvalue":float(np.linalg.eigvalsh((Gn+Gn.T)/2).min()),
+       "condition_number_A_plus":float(np.linalg.cond(Ap)),
+       "condition_number_A_minus":float(np.linalg.cond(An)),
+       "maximum_direct_matrix_formula_error":float(max(errors)),
+       "maximum_sparse_query_difference":float(max(sparse_differences)),
+       "all_m_controls_at_m_prediction_difference":float(abs(pf-nf)),
+       "plus_response_change_m_to_2m":float(pv-pf),
+       "minus_response_change_m_to_2m":float(nv-nf),
+       "opposite_ranking_of_two_admissible_actions":bool((pv-pf)*(nv-nf)<0)})
+output={"status":"exact_analytic_construction_and_synthetic_checks_only", "results":results}
+Path(__file__).with_name("high_order_obstruction_results.json").write_text(json.dumps(output,indent=2)+"\n")
+print(json.dumps(output,indent=2))

+#!/usr/bin/env python3
+"""Scalar-only control-map acquisition. Synthetic checks, not apparatus data.
+
+The estimator sees only (u, scalar_response) queries, never the plant matrix.
+Run: python3 check_scalar_acquisition.py
+"""
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import itertools
+import json
+from pathlib import Path
+import numpy as np
+
+
+def response(f0, a, H, u):
+    u = np.asarray(u)
+    z = np.linalg.solve(np.eye(len(u)) + H * u[None, :], np.ones(len(u)))
+    return f0 - np.dot(a * u, z)
+
+
+class ScalarOracle:
+    def __init__(self, f0, a, H, noise=0.0, seed=0):
+        self.f0, self.a, self.H = f0, a, H
+        self.noise = noise
+        self.rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
+        self.records = []
+
+    def __call__(self, u):
+        value = float(response(self.f0, self.a, self.H, u))
+        measured = value + self.noise * self.rng.normal()
+        self.records.append((np.asarray(u).copy(), measured))
+        return measured
+
+
+def acquire(m, oracle, t1=0.5, t2=1.5, t3=1.0):
+    """Fixed-anchor algorithm. Rejects no data silently; reports nonreal pairs."""
+    zero = np.zeros(m)
+    f0 = oracle(zero)
+    a = np.zeros(m, dtype=complex)
+    H = np.zeros((m, m), dtype=complex)
+    pair = {}
+    nonreal = 0
+    margins = []
+    for i in range(m):
+        deltas = []
+        for t in (t1, t2):
+            u = zero.copy(); u[i] = t
+            deltas.append(f0 - oracle(u))
+        d1, d2 = deltas
+        H[i, i] = (d2 / t2 - d1 / t1) / (d1 - d2)
+        a[i] = d1 * (1 + H[i, i] * t1) / t1
+    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(m), 2):
+        ds, rs = [], []
+        for t in (t1, t2):
+            u = zero.copy(); u[i] = u[j] = t
+            delta = f0 - oracle(u)
+            den0 = (1 + H[i, i] * t) * (1 + H[j, j] * t)
+            num0 = (a[i] + a[j]) * t + (a[i] * H[j, j] + a[j] * H[i, i]) * t*t
+            ds.append(delta); rs.append((num0 - delta * den0) / (t*t))
+        p = (rs[1] - rs[0]) / (ds[0] - ds[1])
+        q = rs[0] + ds[0] * p
+        roots = np.roots([a[i], -q, a[j] * p])
+        choices = [(x, (q - a[i] * x) / a[j]) for x in roots]
+        if max(abs(x.imag) + abs(y.imag) for x, y in choices) > 1e-7:
+            nonreal += 1
+        pair[i, j] = choices
+
+    def setpair(K, i, j, choice):
+        K[i, j], K[j, i] = choice
+
+    def probe_triangle(indices, candidates):
+        idx = np.array(indices)
+        u = zero.copy(); u[idx] = t3
+        observed = oracle(u)
+        preds = [response(f0, a[idx], K[np.ix_(idx, idx)], np.full(3, t3)) for K in candidates]
+        residuals = [abs(p - observed) for p in preds]
+        order = np.argsort(residuals)
+        margins.append(float(abs(preds[order[1]] - preds[order[0]])))
+        return candidates[order[0]]
+
+    if m >= 2:
+        setpair(H, 0, 1, pair[0, 1][0])
+    for k in range(2, m):
+        candidates = []
+        for ci, cj in itertools.product(range(2), repeat=2):
+            K = H.copy()
+            setpair(K, 0, k, pair[0, k][ci])
+            setpair(K, 1, k, pair[1, k][cj])
+            candidates.append(K)
+        H = probe_triangle((0, 1, k), candidates)
+    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(2, m), 2):
+        candidates = []
+        for choice in pair[i, j]:
+            K = H.copy(); setpair(K, i, j, choice); candidates.append(K)
+        H = probe_triangle((0, i, j), candidates)
+    return f0, a, H, {"queries": len(oracle.records), "nonreal_pairs": nonreal,
+                       "minimum_triangle_candidate_separation": min(margins) if margins else None}
+
+
+def dissipative_plant(m, seed):
+    """A real strictly dissipative one-port plant, n=m+1 hidden/observed states.
+
+    Build its inverse G. The estimator receives only a scalar one-port oracle.
+    Full symmetric part of G is positive definite, hence so is that of A=G^-1.
+    The hidden block is dense and nonreciprocal.
+    """
+    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
+    H = 2 * np.eye(m) + rng.normal(size=(m, m)) * 0.30 / np.sqrt(m)
+    np.fill_diagonal(H, 2 + rng.uniform(-0.2, 0.2, m))
+    w = rng.uniform(1.0, 2.0, m) / np.sqrt(m)
+    v = rng.uniform(1.0, 2.0, m) / np.sqrt(m)
+    f0 = 4.0
+    G = np.block([[np.array([[f0]]), v[None, :]], [w[:, None], H]])
+    minimum = np.linalg.eigvalsh((G + G.T) / 2).min()
+    if minimum <= 0:
+        raise RuntimeError("generated plant not dissipative")
+    # Diagonal gauge w -> 1; a_i = v_i*w_i.
+    Hg = H * w[None, :] / w[:, None]
+    return f0, v*w, Hg, {"min_symmetric_inverse_eigenvalue": float(minimum),
+                          "plant_condition_number": float(np.linalg.cond(G))}
+
+
+def run_trials():
+    results = []
+    for m in (3, 8, 16, 32):
+        for noise in (0.0, 1e-10, 1e-8, 1e-6, 1e-4):

+                pdiff = pred[:50].real - pred[50:].real

+            results.append({"m": m, "absolute_response_noise_sd": noise,
+                "queries_per_run": info["queries"],
+                "expected_queries": (3*m*m-m+4)//2,
+                "runs": 8, "heldout_configurations_per_run": 100,

+def exact_counterexamples():
+    import sympy as s
+    a = s.Matrix([1, 2, 3])
+    H = s.Matrix([[10, s.Rational(1,5), s.Rational(1,2)],
+                  [s.Rational(3,10), 10, s.Rational(11,10)],
+                  [s.Rational(7,10), s.Rational(13,10), 10]])
+    K = H.copy()
+    K[0,2], K[2,0] = 3*H[2,0], H[0,2]/3
+    def exact(M, u):
+        D = s.diag(*u)
+        return s.Integer(10) - (a.T * D * (s.eye(3)+M*D).inv() * s.ones(3,1))[0]
+    u1,u2,u3 = s.symbols("u1 u2 u3")
+    pair_equal = []
+    for i,j in itertools.combinations(range(3), 2):
+        u=[0,0,0]; u[i]=u1; u[j]=u2
+        pair_equal.append(s.cancel(exact(H,u)-exact(K,u)) == 0)

+    generic_values=[]

+        M=H.copy()
+        for bit,(i,j) in zip(bits, [(0,2),(1,2)]):

+        generic_values.append(exact(M,[1,1,1]))

+    # Every scheduled datum is identical; the interior triple still differs.

+        H5=np.zeros((5,5)); K5=np.zeros((5,5))
+        H5[:2,:2]=np.array([[10,.2],[.3,10]])
+        K5[:2,:2]=H5[:2,:2]

+        for i in range(2):
+            for j in range(2,5):
+                H5[i,j]=K5[i,j]=eps*(1+i+j)
+                H5[j,i]=K5[j,i]=eps*(2+2*i+j)
+        a5=np.array([1.,2.,1.,2.,3.])
+        o=ScalarOracle(10.,a5,H5)
+        acquire(5,o)
+        differences=[abs(response(10.,a5,H5,u)-response(10.,a5,K5,u)) for u,y in o.records]
+        future=np.array([0.,0.,1.,1.,1.])
+        weak.append({"epsilon":eps,"maximum_difference_on_all_scheduled_queries":float(max(differences)),
+                     "difference_on_unqueried_interior_triple":float(abs(response(10.,a5,H5,future)-response(10.,a5,K5,future)))})
+    return {"single_and_pair_response_functions_identical":all(pair_equal),
+            "triple_responses_exact":list(map(str,full_values)),
+            "triple_response_difference_exact":str(full_values[0]-full_values[1]),
+            "four_anchor_orientation_predictions_exact":list(map(str,generic_values)),
+            "four_anchor_orientation_predictions_distinct":len(set(generic_values))==4,
+            "weak_anchor_counterexample":weak}
+

+def direct_plant_check():
+    m=12
+    f0,a,H,physical=dissipative_plant(m,43)
+    G=np.block([[np.array([[f0]]),a[None,:]],[np.ones((m,1)),H]])
+    # This diagonal gauge need not preserve a Euclidean dissipation metric;

+        errors.append(abs(np.linalg.solve(loaded,b)[0]-response(f0,a,H,u)))
+    return {"maximum_direct_loaded_plant_error":float(max(errors)),**physical}
+
+
